title: University asks staff to review some partnerships with China after MI5 warning
content:
Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) has asked staff to review some partnerships with China after a warning from MI5.

In a highly unusual move, the UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage.

MI5 said the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) was a front company working for China's intelligence and security service.

However, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated".

Staff at Queen's have now been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI".

"Work is ongoing within Queen's to do this," an email to staff said.

"However, this may not be obvious through our existing systems and so researchers are also advised to undertake appropriate due diligence to identify the ultimate source of funding for collaborations with Chinese institutions."

MI5 issued the alert for UK universities about CGTRI which it said had "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).

Universities in the UK often collaborate and partner with universities elsewhere in the world to share research and expertise.

But MI5 said it had identified more than 100 UK-linked academics who had contributed to projects funded by Ministry of State Security via CGTRI.

It said that in some cases the researchers would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.

MI5 added that academics who failed to cut ties with CGTRI could ultimately face criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.

As a result, UK universities were advised to immediately review the funding of any research collaboration with China.

A QUB spokesperson told BBC News NI that the university takes "responsibilities around research and national security extremely seriously".

"Queen's University has commenced a review around any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI," they said.

"We have also contacted staff requesting they review any existing or proposed collaborations with them and report any concerns to the relevant Faculty Dean of Research.

"We will keep this situation under review while continuing to support our collaboration, research and innovation projects locally, nationally and internationally."

According to its website, QUB has invested over $10m (£7.56m) in China-related research in areas like sustainable energy, information technology, food security and cancer research over the past decade.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Ulster University said they had no research links with the organisation referenced by MI5.

title: Queen's University students blast off to US for Nasa robotics competition
content:
Could a robot designed by young engineering students from Northern Ireland end up on the Moon?

A team, from Queen's University Belfast (QUB), are heading to Florida later this month to take part in a Nasa 'lunabotics' competition.

Lunabotics is a university-level competition for teams to use the Nasa systems engineering process to design, build, and operate a lunar robot.

The students created a lab-built robot that they will bring to the competition to find out how it would deal with future moon missions.

The robots will be expected to dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles and use the material to form a wall.

Jack Fitzpatrick, who's studying for a PhD in mechanical engineering, said "it's a great feeling" to have been invited and they're looking forward to the opportunity to take part.

The team of 10 QUB students made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year.

They'll be competing at the University of Central Florida against university teams from Australia, India and the US.

Jamie Smith is a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student.

He explained that the team was divided into three groups for software, electronics and mechanical.

Jamie was the software team lead for this project. He said their main task was to control the rover then provide the autonomous capabilities towards it.

And, they had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually got one.

Jack, however, is part of the mechanical side.

"We analyse that something is physically strong enough, it's well built enough to survive this environment, it's going to have the traction to drive in this environment," he explained.

Jamie explained they designed the 52 kg aluminium frame robot rover and took it compete at a competition in Milton Keynes.

"We got on very well. We ended up winning the competition and had great fun," he said.

Then a few weeks later, they were invited to compete at Nasa's international Lunabotics competition.

Jack said that being asked to go was a "great feeling" and "a real opportunity to demonstrate everything that you've learned".

"It's just a great opportunity to represent Northern Ireland, the UK and really Europe abroad as we are the only European team that will be there," Jack explained.

Both of the students said their success was a reflection of both themselves and also the university and the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.

What does the robot actually do?

Jamie explained that the main objective of the rover is that should be able to drive itself around a lunar-simulated room.

"That means it should start at a point, figure out where it is within this room, travel to an excavation point, so in that point, it will pick up then some sand which is meant to be lunar-simulant.

"It'll pick up the sand and then deposit it at another location, and it's meant to do this all by itself."

Jack explained that the purpose of this is to simulate how real rovers carry out these kind of tasks on the moon.

"It's being able to autonomously operate on the moon and build environments for humans to later habitat. And that's the real drive behind why this competition exists," he explained.

So are they feeling confident they can bring home another win?

Jack explained that there have been several precursor competitions in different countries and this competition takes the top tier of those competitions and brings them together "to really showcase the talent" that there is internationally.

"We are the winning team from the United Kingdom competition and we will be representing the UK and, by extension, Europe at this competition."

"We may not win the competition this year but we're building a base upon which we can improve year on year and maybe come back in a few years and really come through with a winning design," he said.

Caolán Boyle, Head of Robotics at QPL, said the team is "exceptionally proud and excited".

He said "hundreds of hours have gone into making the rover mission ready for the event".

title: I was told my baby boy's skin was as fragile as glass
content:
When Ciara's son Ralph was born, he had skin missing from his hands and feet. Doctors said he was as fragile as glass.

Ralph was diagnosed with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), also known as butterfly skin, at a few days old.

Ciara and her partner Lewis had to become experts in the rare genetic disorder, which causes skin to tear or blister at the slightest touch.

"We were new parents, we had never heard about this before and we had basically been told my son was like glass," Ciara, from Arlesey in Bedfordshire, says.

The 30-year-old mum is now calling on the government to increase funding and research into rare skin conditions, with the hope of one day finding a cure.

Five minutes after Ralph was born, following what Ciara describes as a normal pregnancy, she noticed "big raw patches" on his hands and feet.

"My partner Lewis went to the NICU [neonatal intensive care unit] with him and left me with a picture of him," she says.

"I spent the whole time looking at that picture questioning what on earth was going on."

After being put in a heated incubator, Ralph's body broke out in head-to-toe blisters.

Two days later, the couple received a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa, with the specific subtype of junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), of which there are two main forms.

Ralph's form is generally milder, rather than the severe type which can be life-threatening. But there is no cure and limited treatment options.

Ralph's parents grease bottle teats to avoid damaging his mouth and turn his baby-grows inside out to avoid friction from the seams. They spend up to three hours each night replacing bandages on his feet.

"At the start, when he was a newborn, everything felt so heavy. It was really hard to imagine him being happy.

"Doctors from Great Ormond Street were essentially saying 'we need to teach you how to care for him' and we were expected to learn it – the medical professionals around us at the local hospital were learning on the job with us," she says.

What is junctional epidermolysis bullosa?

Young people with the condition are sometimes called "butterfly children", due to their skin's fragility, like a butterfly's wing.

According to DEBRA UK, the charity for people living with the disorder, it leads to blistering across the body, alopecia, malformed fingers and toenails and irregular tooth enamel.

It is caused by a gene mutation, external which results in faulty or missing proteins in layers of the skin and internal organs. Ralph's DNA lacks the instructions for sticking his epidermis (the surface layer of our skin) to the dermis (the next one down).

Two of the most common symptoms, external are pain and itching from frequent and extensive blistering.

Ciara recently started a petition calling for more research into the condition and after reaching 10,000 signatures, she received a response from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The DHSC, which has also been contacted by the BBC for comment, said it had already committed £1.075m over five years for projects specifically related to EB.

It said research had so far covered advanced treatments, symptom management, supportive care and better care co-ordination.

But Ciara worries her son's rare condition could get "left behind" in the world of research.

"It feels like families like ours are the ones being left to connect the dots. It just doesn't feel good enough.

"If enough people knew how devastating this condition is, something would have to happen because no-one, no human in the world, would stand by and allow children to suffer from birth for the rest of their lives.

"If the system in place is working, why are families like ours still having to work so tirelessly to raise awareness, contact researchers and campaign for anything that might improve our children's quality of life?"

Tony Byrne, chief executive officer of DEBRA UK, says research is "not an abstract ambition" for people with butterfly skin, but "the route to less pain, better treatments, and the hope of a cure".

"This petition matters because dedicated, ring-fenced government investment would give researches greater certainty, help promising discoveries move into UK clinical trials and ensure rare conditions are not overlooked," he adds.

Despite how painful the condition is and the need for more research, Ciara says she has finally started to believe that Ralph can live a happy life.

"He is just the most stubborn, funny, resilient little boy. He loves simple things. When the trees move in the wind, it makes him so happy," she says.

"Ralph can have the most awful wounds on his stomach or his elbows and he's still rolling over trying to get toys. He doesn't let anything stand in his way. He's so fragile, but so desperate to move.

"Despite everything he's so happy, he's so smiley. He won't let anything hold him back."

title: 超强厄尔尼诺刺激 这品种价格创9年新高！
content:
9月30日收盘，沪胶主力合约报收于20095元/吨，相比前一交易日，涨幅5.54%。这是2017年3月以来，沪胶主力合约价格首次突破2万元/吨。
现货方面，据百川盈孚市场监测，9月30日，天然 橡胶 国内市场均价约1.94万元/吨，单日上涨853元/吨，年内涨幅26%，同比上涨31%。
作为国内天然 橡胶 龙头，9月30日， 海南橡胶 开盘仅5秒左右即直线涨停，全天未开板，报收于6.37元/股。
天然橡胶价格今年以来震荡上行的主要原因是什么，又会对产业链影响几何？
橡胶价格为何上涨？
多家机构在最新研报中表示，多因素导致的供给收缩是本轮橡胶现货及 期货 涨价的主要原因。
其中，市场普遍将本轮橡胶 期货 和现货拉升的直接触发因素归结为泰国东北部洪灾。据了解，泰国是全球最大的天然橡胶生产国，其产能周期的走向对全球天然橡胶供给具有锚定作用。今年前8个月，泰国橡胶出口同比持续下滑；9月中下旬以来，泰国持续的暴雨又直接干扰该国东北部橡胶产区割胶作业，供给收缩带动橡胶 期货 和现货价格共振上行。
从全球供给来看，据ANRPC数据，7月ANRPC成员国天然橡胶产量环比提升9.24%，同比下降2.11%。其中，越南产量同比大幅下滑，泰国产量增速偏弱，产胶国出口规模收缩。国内市场看，据海关总署数据，8月，我国天然橡胶进口48.6万吨，同比下降6.7%，为6年同期最低。隆众资讯市场监测显示，青岛保税区及一般贸易天然橡胶合计库存连续7周回落，保税区库存降至近年同期低位。同时，原油价格高位运行抬升合成橡胶生产成本，也对天然橡胶价格形成支撑。
在供给预期方面，国家气候中心最新预测，厄尔尼诺正在继续快速发展，预计将在今年11月前后达到峰值，形成一次有监测记录以来最强的超强厄尔尼诺事件。国际市场对厄尔尼诺引发橡胶减产的预期强烈，这是因为天气变化可能会对东南亚天然橡胶主产区造成干旱影响，进而导致东南亚橡胶单产下降。
有行业分析师告诉记者，本次天气扰动之所以被市场高度重视，不仅在于短期减产预期，更深层的原因在于全球天然橡胶供给弹性不足。
公开资料显示，橡胶树从种植到开割大约需6至8年，13至15年才能进入旺产期，产能调节存在滞后性。上一轮长周期，橡胶低价抑制了更新补种，东南亚主产区老龄树占比近年呈逐步提升趋势，叠加部分胶园改种棕榈油等其他经济作物，新增面积有限，供应弹性下降。
“从已知的数据来看，全球天然橡胶供给面临收缩，叠加库存持续去化，橡胶价格对天气扰动的敏感度上升。”上述分析师对记者表示。
慢牛格局是否确立？
展望节后市场，有机构判断，天然橡胶期货上涨并非单纯情绪炒作，供需边际改善构成上涨基础，牛市基础条件正在积累，市场更偏向慢牛格局逐步确立。
申银万国期货表示，产区割胶仍受降雨扰动，泰国原料胶价格坚挺，保税区库存持续小幅去化，国内供应压力减轻，需求端进入传统旺季，但临近国庆，受原料上涨压力，下游开工同环比走低。厄尔尼诺预期仍存，限制后期供应预期，短期胶价走势预计偏强。
现货方面，有分析师对记者表示，需求方面，国庆假期期间，多数轮胎、橡胶制品企业停工检修，市场交投趋于清淡。经销商大多消耗现有库存，高价补货意愿薄弱。短期内，半钢胎可受冬季换胎需求带动，全钢胎或难有新增订单，整体呈现“供应紧，价格高，需求弱”的局面。预计近期天然橡胶价格偏强震荡，后续走势还需重点跟踪东南亚产区天气、轮胎企业复工进度以及涨价落地执行情况。
产业链上下游影响几何？
天然橡胶价格大幅上行，对产业链不同环节形成分化影响。业内人士认为，上游资源端或直接受益，下游轮胎及橡胶制品生产企业则面临成本端压力，盈利水平取决于成本传导能力、库存策略以及套期保值操作情况。
A股上市公司中， 海南橡胶 是唯一的天然橡胶全产业链上市公司，业务覆盖种植、加工、贸易全链条。公司是目前全球最大的天然橡胶种植、加工、贸易企业，主要生产指标稳居全球首位。
海南橡胶 2026年半年报显示，公司在全球范围内经营管理土地490万亩，其中胶园土地380万亩，境内外天然橡胶种植基地共30个；同时，拥有70余年的天然橡胶种植生产经验和成熟稳定的技术管理队伍，拥有一流的胶园“种植—管理—养护—采割”技术，正分阶段推进180万亩省级标准化胶园建设。
同时，海南橡胶在全球拥有57家在产橡胶初加工厂（含受托管理的KM公司），分布在多个国家和地区，年加工产能约217万吨（含受托管理的KM公司）。公司初加工产品包括全乳胶、浓缩乳胶、烟片胶、印尼标胶等，其中全乳胶、20号标胶是上海期货交易所认证的交割标的。
天然橡胶产业链下游以轮胎为代表，天然橡胶占轮胎生产成本比重较高，胶价上涨直接增加企业原材料成本。
据记者了解，“十一”长假前，国内大部分轮胎企业已陆续官宣10月调价函，产品涨价幅度从2%至5%不等。值得关注的是，部分轮胎生产企业自8月以来，已经两次上调产品价格。
“头部轮胎企业可以通过产品提价、优化产品结构、海外产能布局、长单锁价、开展套期保值等方式对冲成本冲击，若成本能够向下游传导，则利润受冲击有限；相对来说，中小轮胎企业承受的成本压力会更为突出。”有轮胎生产企业的相关人士对记者表示。

title: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
content:
Brazilians have begun voting in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names.

The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, will be challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro.

In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.

Here's what you need to know.

The man not on the ballot

Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election.

Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.

Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election.

At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.

When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.

What do the polls say?

While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.

BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.

The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less.

If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October.

The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out.

BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all.

Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot.

Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.

What does Lula stand for?

Lula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already.

He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família.

The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.

Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.

Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.

When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month.

There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.

His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.

Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.

During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls.

What is Bolsonaro promising?

Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019.

The younger Bolsonaro is running for the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) and, while he is widely seen as less confrontational than his father, he is appealing to the followers of the older Bolsonaro by promising to broadly continue in his footsteps.

During his time in the Senate, the trained lawyer has advocated a tough-on-crime stance, calling for longer sentences and laxer gun laws, arguing that "decent citizens" should be able to defend themselves from criminals.

He has successfully lobbied for the US to declare Brazil-based criminal gangs Comando Vermelho (CV) and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a move that was opposed by Lula.

The younger Bolsonaro has also courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry as part of his campaign.

He has said that he will cut what he says are unnecessary regulations and "get the state off farmers' backs".

Quizzed in an interview with Globo in August on whether he still believed - as he had said in 2019 - that climate change did not exist, he acknowledged that there had been "extreme climate events", but insisted that these events were "cyclical".

Flávio Bolsonaro has actively courted Trump and members of his administration by portraying himself as a loyal ally during a meeting at the White House in May.

More recently, he promised to join the US-led anti-crime alliance that the Trump administration has dubbed "Shield of the Americas", should he be elected.

What are the main issues worrying voters?

Up until a few months ago, Brazilians told pollsters that crime and security were their main concerns.

But in the weeks leading up to the election, a scandal involving a jailed banker accused of orchestrating one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases has pushed corruption to the top of the list.

The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, is well connected and has ties to many powerful people in Brazil - both on the political right and left.

Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).

Police have since then opened an investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for suspected corruption and money laundering over the financing of the film.

But pollsters say Lula's campaign was also hurt by the Vorcaro scandal, after alleged links emerged between the disgraced banker and an ally of Lula, the Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

Moraes is the man who presided over Jair Bolsonaro's trial and has made a number of subsequent rulings about the conditions of his detention.

A police report suggested that Vorcaro had made numerous calls and sent a number of messages to a phone number which officers say is linked to Moraes.

The investigators say Vorcaro asked the person with whom he was communicating for help avoiding arrest.

Moraes has denied any wrongdoing but these latest revelations mean that, in the crucial weeks before the election, attention shifted away from the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro to those against the Supreme Court justice.

Lula has tried to distance himself from Moraes, saying that "no one is above the law", but his rival has already pounced on the allegations against the judge to make political hay.

"Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes," Flávio Bolsonaro told his supporters at a rally, using the right's intense dislike of the judge to shore up his own support.

title: 贝森特“灭火”：美债收益率上升属全球现象，驳斥AI泡沫担忧
content:
美国财政部长贝森特为近期国债收益率攀升进行辩护，并对人工智能泡沫论予以驳斥，同时暗示美国政府未来或将向更多盟友国家提供金融援助。
本周10年期美债收益率一度触及2002年以来最高水平，尽管如此，贝森特在接受媒体采访时表示， 当前利率走势是全球共性现象，无需过度担忧。
贝森特强调这一轮上升并非美国独有，市场没有出现抛售美债、转购德国或日本国债的迹象。
在经济层面，他认为伊朗战争带来的外部冲击掩盖了美国经济的内在韧性，消费支出强劲，中位薪资增速与通胀基本持平。
此番表态发生在美国债市持续数月承压的背景下。高油价、财政健康状况的忧虑以及AI支出激增共同推高借贷成本，抵押贷款利率已远超7%，柴油价格创历史纪录，通胀压力对普通选民的冲击正转化为特朗普政府和共和党在11月中期选举中面临的政治风险。
收益率上升：全球联动而非美国独有
贝森特在采访中明确区分了“系统性上升”与“异常上升”的概念。他说：
如果是某种特有的异常上升，我会感到担忧，但我们并未看到这种情况。
他同时坦承：
我无法控制债券市场，我能做的是让人们放慢脚步、冷静思考。
周五公布的疲软就业数据为市场带来一定喘息，但此前美债已遭受数月抛售，10年期基准利率短暂升至逾二十年高位。
贝森特将当前压力部分归因于伊朗冲突带来的燃料价格上涨，并预计随着战争进入第八个月，能源冲击终将消退，“油价将得到更充分的供应。”
开放更多“阿根廷式”金融救援，驳斥AI泡沫
在外交金融政策方面，贝森特为特朗普政府对阿根廷的干预行动进行了辩护，并表示不排除未来对其他国家实施类似救援。
去年，美国出手买入比索，并向总统Javier Milei政府提供200亿美元互换额度，帮助阿根廷稳定汇率、避免全面经济危机。贝森特说：
我认为阿根廷的稳定推动了拉丁美洲发生历史性转变，前所未有地有如此多拉丁美洲国家与美国站在一起，那么我们能否再次这样做？当然可以。
他还提及美国协助日本支撑日元，包括两国自1998年以来首次协调联合买入日元干预行动。
针对市场对AI支出过热、存在泡沫的担忧，贝森特予以正面回应。
他认为，微软、谷歌和Meta等头部科技企业正在投入大量资本，并为Anthropic、OpenAI等公司带来可观的营收增长，这与无基本面支撑的泡沫存在本质区别。
在他看来， AI投资热潮具有扎实的商业逻辑，而当前宏观层面的紧缩压力更多源于地缘政治的能源冲击。随着伊朗冲突最终平息，能源价格回落，这一外部扰动因素有望逐步消退。

title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping of jury trial plan, minister says
content:
The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst-case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences than that would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing the right of defendants to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of being cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

'Swifter justice'

Norris earlier said that he remained committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice.

But he added: "I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course.

"This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.

"Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog."

Andrew Thomas KC - chairman of the Criminal Bar Association, which represents barristers who work in crown and magistrates courts - said the profession was "delighted".

"Justice needs juries," he said. "Nothing inspires more public trust than 12 ordinary citizens from all walks of life deciding the facts of a case together.

"We are also pleased that the government is going ahead with important changes in the bill to protect victims and witnesses at trial. These include new powers to prevent unfair questioning about a complainant's behaviour and to support witnesses to give their best evidence."

But Thomas warned plans to keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates could backfire - not least because of a shortage of magistrates.

"The proposal to strip defendants of their right to elect a crown court trial, combined with doubling magistrates' sentencing powers to two years, would shift 25,000 cases a year - including 5,500 jury trials - out of the crown court," he said.

"These are not minor offences. It includes serious and sensitive cases including assaults, sexual assaults, child abuse and grievous bodily harm. Our volunteer magistrates do an excellent job but they are completely unequipped to try complex, multi-day trials.

"It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time."

Claire Waxman, victims' commissioner for England and Wales, said victims were "being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves argued would not be [enough]".

Barrister Karl Turner, a Labour MP who was suspended from the parliamentary party after he criticised the government's plans to reform jury trials, thanked Burnham "for his support during my campaign".

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court."

Liberal Democrat justice spokeswoman Jess Brown-Fully added the proposal "should never have been introduced in the first place", while Green MP Sian Berry said it was "a victory for justice and fairness".

title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you
content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors

"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."

That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.

His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.

Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.

It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.

We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.

The Rob and Romesh bromance

The dynamic between Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan is one of the most enjoyable to watch play out this year.

As well as being great friends in real life, they have also worked together repeatedly, including in their travel show, Rob & Romesh Vs.

They've also frequently made joint appearances on panel shows such as Mock the Week.

But their friendship could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said ahead of the show.

"Rob is one of my best friends, and we've worked together for a decade now, but I still won't be able to trust it," he said.

"I mean, he's just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity."

What role would you play? Take our quiz to find out

Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday

The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

Joe and James are also friends (for now)

Joe Lycett has said publicly that he's friends with James Acaster, and the pair have a running joke about how everyone gets them confused.

They’ve also worked together on the TV show Travel Man.

Lycett is also friends with Joanne McNally, external - he's described her as "one of my favourite people in the world".

But those loyalties could be about to be tested, especially now that Acaster has been recruited as a traitor (anyone remember how things panned out for "good friends" Alan Carr and Paloma Faith...?)

Lots of them are on the comedy circuit

There are SO many comedians in this year's series.

And they are all likely to know each other. In addition to the alliances above, Joe Lycett was on the TV show Last One Laughing with Rob Beckett.

Joanne McNally and Romesh Ranganathan appeared on game show Unacceptable together, and James Acaster went on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast.

Speaking ahead of the show, McNally insisted she and her fellow comedians "haven't been in cahoots at all".

"We know that we're more than willing to throw each other under the bus," she said.

As for Acaster, he's admitted the other comedians are his “biggest threat” when it comes to being detected as a traitor.

“Romesh, Joe, Rob know me really well. They all know that I don’t change my mind overnight,” he said, as he pondered whether to turn and help fellow traitor Richard E Grant clear his name.

Maya has rubbed shoulders with several of the stars

It won’t surprise you that the two broadcasters of the group - Maya Jama and Amol Rajan - have met their fair share of the other stars before.

Rajan had previously hosted both Michael Sheen and Joe Lycett on the Radio 2 Breakfast show, and also interviewed Romesh Ranganathan on BBC Asian Network.

He's also been joined on the One Show on separate occasions by Ross Kemp, Miranda Hart and James Blunt - and earlier this year, he discussed AI on stage with Hannah Fry.

But in the end, Rajan became the first player to be murdered, before we really got to see the impact of those past connections.

Meanwhile, Maya Jama is best known for hosting Love Island, but she's also popped up in loads of other places - including at this year's Brit Awards, where she presented an award with James Blunt.

She's also been on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast, attended Milan Fashion Week with Leigh-Anne Pinnock, and she, Joe Lycett and James Acaster all appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

But Jama played down her connections on Celebrity Traitors, saying ahead of the show: “I've met a few people in the cast, but nobody really knows me, so we're all starting from scratch.”

Bella and Sebastian are Westeros alumni

Usually the younger celebs in the castle tend to know fewer people, but Bella Ramsey is pretty well connected.

Notably, Ramsey and another younger cast member, Sebastian Croft, both starred in season six of Game of Thrones.

Ramsey also worked with James Blunt on the film Sunny Dancer, was interviewed by James Acaster on his Off Menu podcast - and had a funny chat about their "vegan-ish" diet with Romesh Ranganathan on The Jonathan Ross Show.

Ahead of the show, Croft said he didn't know many people aside from Ramsey before joining.

"One of the other things I'm excited about is this will be the first time I'm playing with people who, on the whole, don't know me and don't know how I work,” he said.

Richard and Jerry go way back

“I just don't believe Richard's a traitor. I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour.”

That was American model Jerry Hall, speaking after actor Richard E Grant came under (admittedly self-inflicted) pressure in the opening episode of the series.

As well as being neighbours, the pair are linked in lots of other ways.

Grant was pictured leaving Hall's wedding to Rupert Murdoch in 2016; in 2003, they were pictured together at Chelsea Flower Show, and they also acted in children's film Tooth back in 2004.

"It was ridiculous,"Jerry said of the film. "We had such a laugh, and I went on holiday with him earlier this year, just after Christmas to Africa with some friends. And we danced all night. We had so much fun! Little did we know back then that we'd both be here [on Celebrity Traitors]."

Now they've taken the next step and moved in together, will they be arguing over who takes the bins out? We are here for it.

Romesh and Julie are connected by The Weakest Link

Yes, you know Romesh Ranganathan is the host of The Weakest Link.

But did you know actor Julie Hesmondhalgh is the voiceover narrator for the quiz show?

Here are a few other connections you may not have known about.

Hesmondhalgh and Michael Sheen both fronted Papyrus's online child safety campaign back in 2020.

YouTuber King Kenny was one of 10 online stars competing in the game show Would You Rather, hosted by Romesh Ranganathan.

And singers James Blunt and Leigh-Anne Pinnock are both Brit Award winners. Both being successful musicians, it wouldn't be surprising if they have mingled together at events over the years.

Where does this leave those with fewer friends?

While some of the celebrities have known each other for 30 years, others have no friends in the castle at all.

My Mad Fat Diary actor Sharon Rooney and Industry star Myha'la, for instance, have fewer connections than the others.

And that can be a disadvantage. Remember Niko Omilana and Ruth Codd last year?

After they were banished early on, a theory spread on social media that they were voted out because the other celebrities didn't know them that well.

But it can definitely go both ways.

Leigh-Anne Pinnock has said the fact she doesn't know many people might actually help her.

"I think I'm at a slight advantage because people just know me as Leigh-Anne from Little Mix, and they don't really know my personality that well," she said.

What's clear is that these prior connections are "exactly the sort of thing" that makes Celebrity Traitors so fascinating, as TV reporter Siobhan Synnot told me.

But - like Pinnock - she agrees that having loads of friends doesn't necessarily end up helping you.

"Quite often in The Traitors," she says, "that familiarity becomes a disadvantage".

Players, you have been warned.

title: Gentle parenting, helicopter or snowplough – is there really a best way to be a parent?
content:
Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children.

"Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh.

Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries.

But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever".

Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world."

"I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai.

Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone.

Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support.

And it's not just the early years.

Research from the charity Action for Children found that many parents of teenagers who initially contacted the charity for help with school avoidance, ADHD or mental health, often went on to describe their own anxiety, exhaustion and uncertainty of how to parent with empathy and patience when close to burnout.

Faced with an array of parenting philosophies, or "brands" to choose from, is all of this advice helping parents or making them more anxious? And is there really a best way to parent? Or, as we strive to become the perfect parent, are we losing our intuition?

The rise of parenting brands

Parents today are confronted by parenting styles including "helicopter parenting", which is focused on closely monitoring and protecting children from harm, and "tiger parenting", which involves strict parenting and high expectations for achievement. There are also "snowplough parents", who try to remove obstacles from their child's path, and "dolphin parents", who aim to be firm but flexible.

Author Matilda Gosling, who wrote Evidence‑Based Parenting, says many of the parenting fads or trends complicate what should be a straightforward relationship between a parent and child.

"Some parents think 'I need to be a snowplough parent and plough all of these obstacles out of the way'."

"But it really complicates what is actually a fairly fundamental part of being human, which is that you are warm and you love your children and you put in place some boundaries around them."

Gosling believes parenting trends often represent a pendulum swing, with one generation trying to correct what it believes the previous one got wrong.

"Throughout history, you get these swings from one extreme to the other," she says.

Gentle parenting is seen by some as the latest swing away from a strict, detached parenting style popular in the 1990s, which often relied on controlled crying, the naughty step and time out.

It is built around understanding, empathy and respect but also emphasises the importance of boundaries.

The different parenting styles

One of the most widely studied models of parenting comes from developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind.

Baumrind identified three parenting styles, later expanded to four: authoritative (high warmth and high control), authoritarian (low warmth and high control), permissive (high warmth and low control), and neglectful (low warmth and low control).

"Authoritative is the gold standard," says Gosling who has looked at more than 1,000 studies.

Research has found that children raised with an authoritative approach, combining warmth with clear boundaries, tend to achieve better academic results, have higher self-esteem and stronger social skills.

But where gentle parenting fits within that framework is disputed. Gosling believes that it falls on the permissive side.

"It's very much child-led. The child ends up having so much control that there's no sense of safety coming from the outside."

However, Sarah Ockwell-Smith, who is widely credited with coining and popularising the term 'gentle parenting', strongly disagrees.

"It [gentle parenting] is not remotely permissive," she says, putting it firmly in Baumrind's authoritative category. Clear boundaries are "super important".

Social media, however, is flooded with memes of exhausted parents calmly negotiating with a child having a supermarket meltdown, something Ockwell-Smith finds deeply frustrating.

"I have to step away from the Instagram reels and the TikToks because I just want to comment, 'This is not gentle parenting'".

"You have house rules, family limits, discipline and consequences. But the difference is we look at discipline as learning and teaching rather than punishing."

Toddler tantrums and teenage behaviour, she argues, should be viewed through a lens of ongoing brain development, not 'they're being naughty' or 'they hate me'.

But despite the term being popular, Ockwell-Smith believes that gentle parenting is still a fringe movement and that authoritarian parenting remains the dominant style.

The pressure to get parenting 'right'

Around 80 years ago, American paediatrician Dr Benjamin Spock published a book called Baby and Child Care, which went on to sell millions of copies and became the main source of advice for mothers for generations.

The opening line was "Trust yourself. You know more than you think..."

The book challenged strict parenting norms of the time and in the following decades parents were offered more advice from an increasing range of voices.

Research into parenting has increasingly focused on the early years - from pregnancy to the age of two when the building blocks for lifelong emotional and physical health are laid down. For parents, that means more advice to navigate competing messages about what is best for their children.

Professor Ellie Lee, the director of the Centre for Parenting Culture Studies, has studied parenting for more than two decades, including research into mothers' confidence and uncertainty around infant feeding.

She says a major shift occurred in the 1990s when parenting became an increasing focus of public policy.

"Politicians started to say 'Parenting's the hardest job in the world. Children don't come with a manual. We need to give parents guidance. Parents need more support. We need parent education'."

Advice began to emerge on almost every aspect of family life, from tummy time, to feeding, to the right buggy, she explains.

Prof Lee argues that while some public health campaigns were necessary, such as advice not to put babies to sleep on their front after research into cot deaths, the growing culture of advice began to make parents paranoid.

"Dr Spock's 'trust yourself' philosophy is now a very counter-cultural piece of advice," she says. "What we say instead is 'always seek help',"

She believes this has made parents more anxious about doing things "right".

"Some of the things that are now presented as really high stakes are not," she says, using examples like breastfeeding exclusively for six months or how much tummy time a child needs.

"It's terrible because parents become completely exhausted."

Ockwell-Smith says the volume of advice can be "deafening and confusing".

"Actually, parents should just learn themselves and go on intuition," she says.

Others point out that there is also a problem of advice being given that is altogether wrong. Ruth Watts is a health visitor who began sharing content on social media after becoming concerned about misinformation online.

She had seen "experts" advise parents to wean babies onto solids early, offer treatment advice for tongue tie or allergies without medical training, and tell parents to put babies in their own rooms before six months.

Many families, she argues, are working longer hours while at the same time health services are being stripped back, leaving more parents looking online for breastfeeding, behaviour and sleep support.

"We are looking for that kind of personable, conversational approach from people, rather than reading a website."

More advice or simply more confidence?

Many factors shaping family life remain outside parents' control. A child's temperament, special educational needs, family support, finances and their own upbringing can all influence family life.

While some say parenting hasn't got harder but expectations have, others argue that parents today are facing more complex challenges than in previous generations with growing concerns around young people's mental health.

There are also debates around children spending more time on screens and less time outdoors, while schools are reporting increasing behavioural challenges and lower respect for rules and authority. Prof Lee believes parental confidence is at an all-time low.

"I think parents feel very nervous about disciplining children now because they're worried about how it's going to make them feel," she argues.

The confusion around the "right" way to parent has led some parents to turn to courses for help.

Aymara Lamche-Brennan, who has a 22-year-old daughter, four-year-old son and six-month-old daughter, signed up for a course during the summer when another mother at the school gate mentioned she was attending.

"The flyer said 'it's the toughest job in the world' and I thought yes it is, how can you help?'" Aymara says from her home in London.

"When I had my daughter, I was 19 and I didn't really think much about parenting styles, she was with me everywhere and I just kind of rolled with it, but what I really want to know now is what simple wins are there with parenting?"

Aymara said the Circle of Security course she attended gave her practical tools so she could help her children organise their feelings, take charge when she needs to and recognise when she was becoming stressed.

"It's not telling you how to parent. It's helping you think," says Jennifer Peters, a former social worker and director of the charity Connected Lives which runs courses across London, Derbyshire and Cambridgeshire.

She says most parents want the best for their kids but they don't always know how to get there, and that guidance can be helpful.

"I don't think people need to be bombarded with information but the group experience helps you think, 'oh, it's not just me' and lets you take a step back from it all," Peters says.

Trusting your instincts

Back in Dubai, Rosie says the arrival of her second child changed everything as she realised her sons were "polar opposites" and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

A recent trip home to Birmingham also provided some perspective. Her eldest son was throwing a tantrum, and Rosie found herself wrestling with a familiar worry.

"If I send him upstairs, am I damaging him emotionally? Is he going to develop an attachment disorder because of this?"

But her mum said, 'Just send him upstairs. He can't hit his brother over the head with a horse [if he is upstairs]. Follow through with your actions.'

Rosie is taking this "generational advice" on board and has started "venting on social media" to show other mums that they are not alone.

Looking back on her first few years of being a mum, she said she wished she had known one thing.

"There isn't the perfect parent."

title: Autumn chill to arrive this week as temperatures set to drop
content:
Temperatures are set to drop across the UK during the week ahead, bringing an end to a run of warmer-than-average autumn weather.

By Wednesday, afternoon highs are expected to range from 11C (52F) in northern Scotland to 17C (63C) in southern England.

It will mark a significant change from the summer-like warmth that has brought temperatures of up to 28C over the last week.

If the thermometer fails to reach 20C anywhere in the UK, it will be the first time that has happened since 11 June.

Mild end to weekend before temperatures tumble

In south Wales, the Midlands, East Anglia and southern England, early mist and fog could linger for a while in a few locations on Sunday.

However, once this clears sunny spells are expected.

More cloud will develop in north Wales and northern England with the chance of a few spots of rain.

Northern Ireland will be even cloudier, with some outbreaks of mainly light rain and drizzle.

The wettest weather will be found across Scotland with heavy rain likely in the west, accompanied by wind gusts of 40mph or more in the far north-west.

Temperatures will generally be a few degrees above the seasonal norm and could possibly reach 23C in the sunniest parts of southern England.

A weather front will erratically move southwards during Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

This will bring outbreaks of rain which will generally be heaviest in northern and western parts of the UK and lighter further east.

It is possible that heavier downpours with thunder and lightning could affect southern and south-eastern England on Tuesday night and Wednesday.

As the rain clears southwards cooler air will be left in its wake with daytime temperatures by midweek expected to be at - or even slightly below - the seasonal average.

Some chilly nights are also expected with a touch of frost possible in prone locations.

Check your local temperature forecasts on the BBC Weather website and app.

A warm autumn so far

With meteorological autumn covering the months of September, October and November, the season is now one-third of the way over.

Met Office figures show that it has been a warmer-than-normal autumn so far, with September being the joint-fourth warmest on record for the UK as a whole.

With a mean average temperature of 14.6C, it was 1.6C above the long-term average.

The longer-range prospects for autumn predict more of the same.

It is forecast to be warmer and wetter than average with the chance of stormy weather later in the season - partly due to the developing very strong El Niño in the Pacific.

The UK is on track for one of its warmest years on record, according to the Met Office.

title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
content:
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.

Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.

Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.

On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.

Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.

The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.

But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.

Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.

The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.

Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.

"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.

Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.

We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.

Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.

"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.

The new rules have divided opinion.

Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.

One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.

''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''

In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.

"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.

But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.

Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.

"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.

Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.

"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.

"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.

For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.

"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."

Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.

Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.

But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.

Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.

The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.

He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.

"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.

For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.
