title: 贝森特自称是马斯克的超级粉丝
content:
美国财长贝森特在周六播出的一次采访中自称是埃隆·马斯克的“超级粉丝”，并再次就马斯克在“政府效率部”任职期间两人曾在白宫发生冲突的传闻进行了澄清。
贝森特在谈到马斯克时说：“ 我是马斯克的超级粉丝，就他试图对政府做的事情而言，我非常支持。 我们有点像一支运动队。你可以在更衣室里争论，但你们一起走上赛场，你们都在做同样的事情。 他太了不起了。就像，他正带着我们去火星。”

title: 贝森特称本周伊朗不会有石油在海上运输
content:
美国财长斯科特·贝森特表示，本周伊朗将没有任何石油在海上运输，也不会有相关收入；华盛顿方面正加大力度，实施他所形容的旨在从经济上孤立德黑兰的“前所未有的行动”。
“这是自他们开始开采石油以来的历史上第一次，本周将没有任何伊朗石油在海上运输，”贝森特在周六播出的一档采访中说道，“他们将没有任何收入。”
贝森特表示，这种经济压力是针对伊朗采取的一系列蓄意军事和经济措施的后续行动。
“我们采取了‘动能’行动（即军事打击），摧毁了他们的海军和空军，大幅削弱了他们的无人机和导弹能力，并粉碎了他们重建这些力量的可能性，”他说。
“随后，我们转向了总统所称的‘铁墙’和封锁策略——这是我们从未做过的，”贝森特补充道，“而现在，我们正在实施‘经济弃儿行动’（ Opera tion Economic Outcast），以前所未有的方式在经济上孤立他们。”

title: 'Incredible' Red Bull upgrade enlivens F1 in Malaysia
content:
Even Lewis Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second place, fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen has dominated the weekend so far on Formula 1's return to the Sepang track for the first time since 2017.

Hamilton joins him on the front row to revive memories of their no-holds-barred title battle five years ago.

But at nearly 0.3 seconds slower in qualifying, and with the pace Verstappen has shown all weekend, Hamilton's mindset on Saturday was to "just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow".

This was Verstappen's first pole position of the year - a remarkable statistic for someone who came within two points of winning a fifth world title last year after one of the all-time great fightbacks.

Red Bull started the year off the pace - the car was on average more than 0.5secs a lap slower than Mercedes in the first half of the year - and for a time there were questions as to whether Verstappen would stick around for 2027.

But after being courted by McLaren, Verstappen signed a two-year contract extension over the summer break, saying he believed in the Red Bull project and didn't mind putting in the work to turn things around.

Verstappen arrived in Malaysia after a run of three consecutive podium finishes, and with Red Bull hoping to prove out an upgrade that had seen them finish less than 0.2secs off victory in Baku last Sunday.

In the tropical heat of Malaysia, around the demanding long corners of this track with perhaps the roughest surface of the season, the upgrade - centred on a new floor - has more than proved its worth.

"It's been an incredible result for us," Verstappen said. "Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us.

"We have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It's simple as that. When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car.

"So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time.

"And then on a track probably where it's all very hot and you want a, let's say, stable balance or connected balance, then that's very important. And that's what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends."

Team-mate Isack Hadjar, who missed the first three races after the summer break with a wrist broken while boxing as part of his training programme, says the car felt transformed when he returned in Baku last weekend.

"I jumped in a car that's way better than when I left it in Budapest," said the Frenchman, who qualified third, but will start eighth after a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts.

"Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference. And the last two weekends have been surprising."

A good car balance should put Verstappen in a good place for a race that will be dominated by tyre degradation in the stifling heat, whether the threatened rain holds off or not.

Where to look for a challenge to Verstappen?

Hamilton, for one, but also Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who under-performed slightly in qualifying because of a combination between an unusual tyre strategy and an error on an early run.

The world championship leader's fourth place becomes third on the grid with Hadjar's penalty, and he can usually be relied upon to be a factor in the race.

Antonelli's main focus will be his advantage over team-mate George Russell, who trails the Italian by 66 points and starts four places behind, his momentum from his Baku win stalled, and somewhat perplexed as to his and his team's lack of pace.

At Mercedes, the bigger question is over the aerodynamic upgrade they brought to the car this weekend.

Mercedes are lagging behind their rivals when it comes to developing their car this season, apparently at least in part because they front-loaded their spend early in the season.

But this first big update since the Canadian Grand Prix in June has not yet proved the step they had expected.

The question is whether that is to do with the parts themselves or the very specific conditions of this weekend, in the heat and on the rough track surface, which is putting the tyres through the mill, and massively limiting the useful laps teams can do in terms of set-up work.

Antonelli said: "With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different. So, we're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best, in the high-speed corner and low-speed corners.

"Our high-speed performance has been very strong this weekend. We were very quick in the high-speed, but in the low-speed we lacked. So, we need to understand why and try to move on and improve."

As for the race, Antonelli said: "Track position is going to be very important. Strategy is going to be really important.

"It's a race where we will attack. Because undercut (stopping first and gaining time on a rival on fresh tyres) is incredibly powerful.

"So whenever there's an opportunity, we should go for maybe an undercut and try to maximise our opportunity.

"Tomorrow might be two stops, three stops. We don't know. But the only thing we know is that it's going to be roasting hot out there."

title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
content:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergency housing legislation through parliament on Friday.

About 50 planned marches are taking place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona .

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," said a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union, where a demonstration has already started. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.

Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported.

One of the biggest demonstration is happening in the capital, Madrid. Estimates of the number of participants varied widely, with the city's Tenants' Union putting it at 500,000, while government officials put the figure at 70,000.

Demonstrators have been camping in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.

One protester, David, told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."

On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".

It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".

The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.

The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

title: Bluetongue restriction zone extension a 'positive thing' for farmers
content:
Restrictions aimed at controlling bluetongue, a virus that affects sheep, cattle and other livestock, are now in force across the whole of Scotland.

The Scottish government said they should be seen as a "positive thing" which would make it easier for farmers to get uninfected animals to market without requiring an individual licence.

The disease, which can be spread by insects such as midges, does not affect people and poses no risk to food safety.

Bluetongue was first detected on farms in south-west Scotland in August and there have now been more than 100 infected animals in 41 locations, including four outside the original restriction zone .

While no danger to humans, Bluetongue can cause fever, swelling, lameness, birth defects and difficulty eating for cows and particularly sheep.

In some cases, animals die or become so ill they have to be euthanised.

Scientists believe the disease probably spread to Scotland after infected midges were blown across the border from England but the risk of transmission is now falling as the midge season draws to a close.

Agriculture Minister Jim Fairlie said extending the restriction zone was a "sensible step" at the current time that would make trading easier for the livestock industry.

It means the whole of Scotland, along with England and Wales, is now covered by a restriction zone, removing the movement barriers between high and low-risk areas because they all now have the same disease status.

He told BBC Scotland News: "It's a bit counterintuitive but extending restrictions is actually a positive thing because it means we've got the ability to move stock freely anywhere in the country now."

October is traditionally a time when many Scottish farmers sell "store" cattle or lambs to other farmers who will fatten them up further.

"We don't want people to be restricted given the fact that it's now at this time where the vets think there's unlikely to be transmission of the disease," Fairlie added.

Farmers must still notify the authorities immediately when an animal displays symptoms.

Infected animals are generally required to remain on-farm for a minimum of 60 days, but the majority of healthy, non-infected animals can be traded.

Fairlie said vaccination remained the most effective way for farmers to protect their animals from the worst effects of bluetongue.

"People need to be thinking about the vaccine programme for next year," he said.

"There is no other way to protect their stock properly so they should be speaking to their vet and looking forward, thinking about what the vaccination programme looks like for them."

Some farmers reported difficulty getting hold of the vaccine this year as demand rose suddenly as cases were reported in England.

Fairlie said having early conversations about next year's vaccination programme would spur on manufacturers to ensure there are adequate supplies.

title: The town where 94% voted for Lula — and some now waver
content:
Michael Pooler in Guaribas

Published October 3 2026

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.

Natalia Duarte remembers the hardship before Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva first became president of Brazil nearly a quarter of a century ago.

There was no piped water in her small town of Guaribas, so every evening she would walk 2km along a sloped trail to fill buckets at a spring, taking one back at a time by the light of an oil lamp. Meals were often just beans and cornflour from the family’s plot.

“Everything started to improve,” the 62-year-old recalled, after Lula took office in 2003 and made the remote community of 4,300 the pilot for his flagship social programme giving cash to poor households. It provided Duarte with money to buy rice, meat and clothes for her children. Clean water was soon supplied by a new treatment system.

“He ended hunger,” the grandmother said. “It was a blessing from God.”

Some 20mn people were lifted out of poverty in the early years of what became Lula’s Bolsa Família (Family Allowance), according to a World Bank estimate.

It earned the leftwing president hallowed status in this corner of the sertão , a vast semi-arid outback in Brazil’s impoverished north-east. Lula won 94 per cent of the municipality’s votes in the 2022 election that narrowly returned him to power more than a decade after his original stint.

But as he seeks a fourth non-consecutive term in what is expected to be a nail-biting contest on Sunday, there are shimmers of disenchantment amid the reverence for the 80-year-old in Guaribas. The local economy has struggled to move beyond welfare and the town’s population has stagnated as some go elsewhere for work.

Despite steady growth and low unemployment nationwide during Lula’s current term, across the country the charismatic former trade unionist has failed to replicate the popularity of his 2003-2010 governments.

There is discontent over security and the cost of living, while many Brazilians had already lost trust in Lula after he was jailed for corruption on convictions that were later overturned. Polls put his main challenger, rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in a run-off, which will take place later this month if no candidate gains an absolute majority on Sunday.

Adversaries say Lula lacks new ideas and has instead relied on expanding handouts and higher public spending, debt and taxes.

There are flickers of disillusionment even in this cradle of the Bolsa Família , a dusty cluster of low-slung buildings off a lonely highway surrounded by scrubland, located in Piauí state.

In 2022, Lula won 69 per cent of the vote across the north-east, the country’s second-most-popular region, but polls project a slight fall in support this time.

For all the older generations’ gratitude towards Lula in Guaribas, some younger voters are sceptical. With the hot streets deserted one afternoon, business was slow at the beauty products store run by Najara Rocha, 28.

“Lots of older people think they still owe him something. He’s already had three terms — I think that’s enough,” she said. Rocha is considering voting for a third candidate: “It’s time for change.”

Rafael Maia, 23, whose family once received Bolsa Família, sat in a barbershop waiting for customers. He intends to spoil his ballot, like in 2022: “Prices are high. Lula has disappointed.”

In 2022, just 193 locals voted for Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, far-right then-president Jair Bolsonaro. They tend to be Evangelical Christians, a growing segment who skew conservative in the majority-Catholic nation. Mônica Alves Duarte, 29, who runs a phone accessory shop and receives Bolsa Família payments, said she opposed Lula’s support for same-sex marriage.

Municipal administrator Henrique Gomes, 61, said the achievements of Lula and his Workers’ Party (PT) in Guaribas were overstated. “It was supposed to be a showcase to the world,” he said. He plans to back the Bolsonaros again.

Locals praise a new ambulance unit and major school refurbishment delivered since Lula returned. However, in a place with small shops but no industry, a common refrain is that the only sources of income are the town hall, Bolsa Família or state pensions.

Lula created the welfare programme by combining and greatly expanding several existing schemes, with payments conditional on child vaccinations and school attendance.

“[It] brought about significant improvements in Brazil, whether access to income for rural populations or better school enrolment,” said Sergio Schneider, a sociologist at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul. “The next step is to include [people] in the labour market. That’s where we run into major barriers.”

Critics of Bolsa Família — which benefits about 50mn individuals and is predicted to cost approximately $34bn, or 1.25 per cent of GDP, in 2027 — say it has bred dependency, making work less attractive. They argue Lula’s PT has cultivated clientelism in the north-east, where almost a third of households are recipients.

Weeks before the election, the president announced a 15 per cent increase in Bolsa Família payments to a monthly average of about $150. Bolsonaro accused him of vote-buying, though the rightwinger, whose father similarly bumped up welfare cheques before the 2022 election, has sworn not to cut the programme.

More than two-thirds of Guaribas residents are beneficiaries of Bolsa Família , analysis of government data suggests, though the number of recipients has fallen by about 10 per cent since 2023. Local social worker Joara Dias, 43, rejects the idea that people take advantage of it.

“Some people get too comfortable, but it’s 5 per cent at most,” she said. “There’s a lack of jobs.”

Policymakers have long struggled to drive sustainable employment in isolated spots of the continent-sized country, especially those with inhospitable climates and scant natural resources. The sertão’ s rainy season is typically only three to four months and droughts can last years.

“In the past, family agriculture was strong, but due to climate change, we’ve lost faith in it. We’ve had four years of lost harvest,” said Dias.

Another charge against the PT is that it has failed to keep up with Brazil’s rising entrepreneurial culture. Hotel and bakery owner Irineu Folha Maia disagrees. The 46-year-old left Guaribas for São Paulo in 2001, swearing never to come back, but says Lula’s policies provided the basis for his business.

“It makes me sad to see people condemning President Lula. We should thank him for the transformation of the town,” he said.

Eraques Folha, 36, said education policies under Lula’s PT, such as bursaries and race or income-based university quotas, had raised aspirations. There were no qualified professionals in town when he was growing up. Now, Guaribas has produced lawyers, accountants, engineers and its first doctor will soon graduate.

After studying in São Paulo on a federal scholarship, Folha returned home to open an IT shop and teach coding at the high school.

There is little doubt Lula will win a hefty majority in Guaribas, but the national result looks like a coin toss.

“It will be like a funeral here if he’s not elected,” Folha said. “He opened up a world of opportunities for the young.”

Natalia Duarte, one of the first Bolsa Família recipients, goes further: “God spare us if he doesn’t win. Suffering will come.”

Additional reporting by Ricardo Lisboa and Beatriz Langella

title: Derelict 'church in the woods' sold at auction
content:
A derelict Grade II listed church located in a wooded area of Leeds has been sold at auction.

St Mary's In The Wood United Reformed Church on Commercial Street in Morley sold for £100,000 earlier this week, auctioneers BTG Eddisons confirmed.

The 19th Century building has not been used for worship since 2008 and fell into disrepair after sustaining extensive fire damage two years later.

A previous planning application lodged with Leeds City Council which has since lapsed proposed the site could be repurposed into a hotel, restaurant and car park.

Later plans to transform the fire-damaged church into 18 apartments also did not come to fruition.

The fire started about 02:30 BST in June 2010 and caused 20 people living nearby to be evacuated to a nearby supermarket due to fears the church steeple could collapse.

In 2023, Leeds City Council purchased the nearby former Sunday School building, which was built in 1900, for use as a "learning and skills centre".

However, the older, Gothic revival-style building, built in 1878, has remained vacant for more than 15 years.

BTG Eddisons could not disclose whether St Mary's was bought by a commercial or private buyer.

title: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage
content:
The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham.

The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up.

That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons.

You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on.

She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core.

She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else".

As we talked about a couple of weeks ago, the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes.

But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return.

Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through.

So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed.

There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet minister warns that it's "the big risk – so easy to slip into an alienating divisive manner – nasty party stuff".

When it comes to policy, and striking the right tone, they warn that Badenoch must "be mindful that she has to win Cheltenham and Maidenhead as well as Clacton".

But Kemi Badenoch is visibly more confident and is aware of the chance in front of her – seemingly unworried about the possible downsides of making an increasingly direct argument to you, eager to stride that mercifully bigger Birmingham stage.

title: UK-Iranian dual national bailed after RAF Fairford incident arrest
content:
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.

Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.

Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."

Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

title: Homemade bomb part of alleged plot on Manchester's Jewish community, court told
content:
Two Iranian men have appeared in court charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade bomb.

Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, were accused at Westminster Magistrates' Court of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September.

One of the buildings they are alleged to have carried out reconnaissance at is the Heaton Park synagogue which was attacked on 2 October 2025.

Both men, who had arrived in the UK by small boat, were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur - the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Salehi and Ahmadyan were remanded in custody by District Judge Nina Tempia until 23 October, when they will appear at the Old Bailey in London.

As part of the investigation, searches were carried out at addresses in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford.

The Metropolitan Police said the men were alleged to have obtained instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquired liquids and other components to make an improvised explosive device.

They are accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps.

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: "Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device.

"The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester's Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue."

'Deeply distressing'

Two British Jews, Melvin Kravitz, 66, and 53-year-old Adrian Daulby, were killed when Heaton Park Synagogue was attacked during last year's Yom Kippur service.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue and began attacking people with a knife while wearing a fake suicide belt.

Westminster Magistrates' Court court heard Salehi and Ahmadyan, who had come to the UK via a small boat in 2020 and 2023 respectively, were alleged to have been "directed and co-ordinated" by another Iranian individual "most likely operating within Iran".

Salehi had previously claimed asylum in Germany and spent five years there, the court heard. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2023 and currently has leave to remain until July 2028.

His co-accused arrived via small boat in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim, the court heard.

The men, wearing grey tracksuits, stood in the dock of court five.

Salehi and Ahmadyan respectively spoke through their Kurdish and Farsi translators only to confirm their name, date of birth and addresses.

Prior to their court appearance, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the news that two Iranian men had been charged would be "deeply distressing" to Manchester's Jewish community as the city marked the first anniversary of the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

She said "the fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago" was a reminder of the "importance of work to tackle illegal migration".

"We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security," she added.

title: China launches anti-dumping probe into European chemical exports
content:
Edward White in Shanghai and Henry Foy in Brussels

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

Beijing has launched an anti-dumping investigation into European exports of a chemical used for dyes and pharmaceuticals as tensions rise over China’s massive trade surplus with the bloc.

The commerce ministry in Beijing said on Saturday that it had started an investigation into p-nitrotoluene, which is also used in pesticide and pigment production, after a complaint from Chinese industry.

The investigation marks the latest tit-for-tat measure between Brussels and Beijing after trade tensions flared again in recent weeks.

The EU opened three anti-dumping investigations into chemicals from China last week. It also began consulting on a new diversification tool that would seek to reduce imports from China.

It comes just ahead of crunch talks between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, commerce minister Wang Wentao, in Beijing this month.

The EU in June set an October deadline for progress in reducing its trade deficit with China, which is now running at €1bn a day.

Brussels has warned that without any action it could resort to new trade measures, which are set to be debated at a summit of EU leaders at the end of October.

The European Commission declined to comment.

The FT reported last month that among the initiatives proposed, the EU has asked China to restrict its exports of plug-in hybrid vehicles voluntarily, as well as restrain exports of some chemicals.

According to the commerce ministry, from 2022 to 2025 European exports of p-nitrotoluene were at high levels while prices declined by 60 per cent, meeting the grounds for an investigation under both Chinese and World Trade Organization rules.

The Chinese move also follows a warning from Brussels to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain would need to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely with EU trade policy if it wants to avoid “made in Europe” barriers on exports to the bloc.

EU officials have argued that Chinese controls on rare earth exports, introduced last year as part of China’s retaliation against US President Donald Trump, have unfairly hit European companies.

Over recent years, the EU has targeted Chinese industrial products with higher tariffs while China has sought to influence EU member governments by hitting agricultural interests, including dairy products, pork and cognac.

title: Europe Express: Lies and statistics
content:
Ben Hall

Published October 3 2026

Welcome back. It’s been a big week in French politics and a tough one for far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next year’s presidential election.

Let’s start with the statistics.

The sell-off in French debt accelerated this week with yields on 10-year government bonds climbing to 4.9 per cent, a rise of 130 basis points since early July (more than double the increase for UK debt). The surge in borrowing costs only adds to the impossible arithmetic — and impossible politics — of deficit reduction in France.

The higher the yields go, the more the public finances become the defining issue in the campaign. This is not to the Rassemblement National leader’s advantage given the party’s promises of massive tax cuts and flaky plans to cut spending. France’s fiscal squeeze could test its claims to be a responsible party of government — to destruction, its mainstream opponents hope.

I’m at [email protected]

Reality check

“Reality is catching up with us,” said prime minister Sébastien Lecornu, as he warned about spiral debt-servicing costs on the eve of his 2027 budget . The interest bill will rise to €73bn next year, up by a fifth on 2026. That bill will grow to €124bn by 2030, according to a report (in French) by a commission led by four independent economists — Xavier Jaravel, Xavier Ragot, Jean-Luc Tavernier and Natacha Valla — in July. Their calculations are already out of date. But their report provides a lucid explanation of France’s predicament.

On current policies, they say, France’s deficit will keep rising to 6.8 per cent of GDP by the end of the decade because of surging interest rates and the increasing costs of an ageing population. Debt will hit 122 per cent of GDP next year and keep on rising to 131 per cent by the end of the decade. France has to run to stand still.

Achieving debt sustainability by the end of the next five-year presidential term would require bringing the deficit to 3 per cent of GDP (a small primary surplus minus debt servicing costs). The four economists said this would require annual savings of €126bn by 2032, with the effort frontloaded during the term. In the three months since their report, that number has risen to €140bn.

None of the presidential candidates has a plan for savings on that scale. As Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, told La Croix newspaper this week, “when your debt is close to 120 per cent of GDP and not on course to be brought under control, it is a serious matter.”

Time for a rule

Le Pen knows she needs to bolster her party’s credibility on public finances. Having long opposed any budget constraints, such as those enforced by the EU, she has now come round to the idea. Writing in L’Opinion on Thursday, Le Pen said she would seek to enshrine a public deficit ceiling in the constitution (a variable number but probably around 2.5 per cent). To get to that objective from the current level of 5.5 per cent, her “golden rule” would require a minimum 0.5 percentage point reduction each year.

Blaming President Emmanuel Macron for the “catastrophic” state of the public finances, she boasted that the RN was now the only party willing to get to grips with the problem.

But a debt rule matters less than a credible plan for the tax rises or spending cuts needed to meet it. The far-right is expected to unveil its new proposals next week. Previous iterations of its annual “shadow budget” beg a lot of questions. The shadow 2026 budget included tax cuts worth some €47bn offset by spending reductions of €88bn. Many of the proposed cuts were questionable: ending benefits for foreigners and withholding half of France’s budget contribution to the EU are legally doubtful. There was also no indication of where a second year of savings would come from — pensions and welfare remain off limits.

Lost ticket?

Now to the “lies”.

RN president Jordan Bardella, who Le Pen touts as her future prime minister, was engulfed in scandal this week when investigative news site Mediapart alleged he had made multiple antisemitic statements in private messages as a young activist in the party. The claims threaten to undo the leadership’s efforts in recent years to “detoxify” the party by rooting out racist and antisemitic elements.

Bardella vehemently denied the allegations, calling them a fabrication and a political assassination attempt. Le Pen said the claims were a “secret service operation”. But on Thursday Mediapart hit back , publishing a dossier with excerpts from messages and a detailed explanation of how it corroborated the evidence, including a cache of messages from Meta that was certified by a legal officer. Bardella is sticking to his line that the claims are a fraud, but he looks like damaged goods.

With debt markets on fire and a joint ticket with Bardella potentially going up in smoke, it’s been a bad spell for Le Pen. But the real flames this week were burning outside high schools across France, where students protesting against underfunded education, egged on by the far left, clashed with police. Shocking scenes were beamed around the world. It was a perfect addition to the RN narrative of an impotent state before a country in chaos.

Vladimir Putin has personally told his military commanders to abandon the rules of war, Volodymr Zelenskyy tells Christopher Miller in an interview from a bombed-out Kyiv school.

title: 'Perimenopause cost me my job and family life'
content:
For three years, Sally Williams struggled to understand what was happening to her as her mental health deteriorated and her life fell apart, spending almost 11 months in hospital across eight admissions.

She left her finance job, was separated from her teenage son and found herself fighting for her life, unaware her symptoms could be linked to perimenopause.

"No one joined the dots," Williams said. "It was only me... I joined the dots and it was transformational to start hormone replacement therapy and literally come back to life."

Williams, who initially self-diagnosed, wants other women to be aware of perimenopause, the years leading up to menopause, which she described as the "danger zone".

Perimenopause, external, which commonly begins around the age of 46, is when women experience menopause symptoms while still having periods.

Symptoms can include anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, hot flushes and irregular periods, with some women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to help alleviate the symptoms.

When her symptoms began in her late 40s, Williams, from the Wychavon area, said doctors she saw initially thought she had depression.

"I had multiple attempts on my life, two significant ones, one where I was in a wheelchair for three months for polytrauma, and this was in Covid, so there were no visitors. I had no contact with anyone," she explained.

"I had to leave my job. This was at perimenopause time. My message to women is that, menopause is not the danger zone, it's the run up, it's the 45 to 54."

For Williams, who said she was "unrecognisable" before her eventual diagnosis, it was HRT which eventually helped her, but she said it may not be for everyone.

The drug, which isn't suitable for some women, tops up and stabilises oestrogen levels, sometimes in combination with a synthetic or bioidentical version of progesterone.

Williams is set to speak about her hard fought menopause diagnosis at Meno Fest at Worcester Rugby Club on 7 October, external, as part of Menopause Awareness Month.

The free event is being held with the aim of helping people to gain greater understanding of how perimenopause and menopause can affect every aspect of life from physical and mental health to relationships, work and family life.

Williams told the BBC of how isolated she became during the "run-up" to menopause.

"I lost my job. I didn't see my friends, my family for three years and I was a recluse. I was self neglecting. And my son, who was in his teens, I probably saw him three times," she explained.

"He had leave his school and his friends and he had to go and live with his dad because he couldn't see me. I couldn't care for him."

It was also important that men recognised what was happening to women during perimenopause, she added.

"I think men need to come into the conversation as well, and I'm not just talking husbands and partners, I'm talking sons," she said.

"It was devastating and there's relationships that have been broken that will never be put back together. I'm very sad about that."

title: Chart of the Week: What’s driving the global bond sell-off?
content:
Hakyung Kim

Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

This article is an on-site version of our Unhedged: Chart of the Week newsletter. You sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Saturday, or explore all FT newsletters

Good morning. Sovereign bond yields have been rising all year, and in the past few weeks the pace has accelerated across most developed markets. But there is not a clear consensus about what’s driving the sell-off. Looking at the most cited factors — inflation and indebtedness — across various countries reveals a mixed picture.

Mapping debt-to-GDP ratios against year-to-date increases in 10-year yields reveals a loose positive relationship. But there are exceptions, such as South Korea, which has a relatively low debt-to-GDP ratio of 52 per cent, but a jump similar to that of Italy, whose public debt sits at a staggering 137 per cent of GDP. Adding inflation rates offers only a little extra clarity. Italy and Spain recently both had annualised inflation readings above 4 per cent, yet their yield increases have lagged behind those of French sovereign bonds, despite France’s tamer inflation rate of 3 per cent.

Growth is another part of the equation. The steady expansion in US real GDP helps explain why its yields have risen more than those of Italy, which has higher debt and more inflation. Finally, there’s the unquantifiable variable: political risk. French bond yields have surged to levels near those of the European debt crisis, as election uncertainty comes on top of a worsening fiscal situation.

The biggest outlier is, of course, Japan. The yield on the 10-year JGB has surged by nearly one percentage point in 2026, an increase comparable to that of Gilts and Italian debt. Yet Japanese inflation came in at just 1.9 per cent in August — the lowest on our list. Historical context is important. While other countries would be pleased with a 1.9 per cent inflation rate, decades of deflation in the Asian nation have made these “normal” inflation levels, alongside a weak yen and energy shock, a bigger jolt to the economy.

title: Trains cancelled after bedbugs found on board
content:
A number of train services were cancelled after drivers discovered bedbugs in their cabs.

Carriages on two affected trains were locked to isolate passenger areas from the cabs, said Southeastern, which operates services in Kent, East Sussex and Greater London.

The rail firm said the trains only remained in service while they "returned to a suitable location for inspection and if necessary, treatment".

The cancellations took place on mainline routes after the bugs were spotted on 22 September. None of the insects were found on any High Speed 1 trains, it added.

In a social media post, Southeastern said the affected trains were based at the West Marina Depot in Hastings, the terminus point for trains from London.

Services on the route go via Battle, Tunbridge Wells and Sevenoaks.

A spokesperson for the firm said trains and stations are cleaned "thoroughly" so passengers can "travel safely and with confidence".

Oly Turner, head of drivers at Southeastern, said: "We have a great relationship with our drivers, who have helped hugely in cooperating with us over these isolated incidents.

"When we receive reports such as these we check trains thoroughly before they are put back into service when given the all clear.

"Cases have been contained to the drivers' cabs in only two of our trains and no bed bugs have been identified in areas for passengers."

title: Boy, 6, who died in van crash was 'loved more deeply than words could ever express'
content:
A six-year-old boy who died when he was struck by a van outside of his home has been named as Harrison Glynne Jones.

In a tribute on a fund-raising page launched to support his family, he was described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character with a personality that could light up a room", and who had been "loved more deeply than words could ever express".

Officers were called to reports of an incident involving a white Ford Transit Tipper and a child on Mill Road in Llanfairfechan, Conwy county, after 17:00 BST on Thursday, where Harrison was pronounced dead at the scene.

North Wales Police said a 39-year-old man had been arrested and later released under investigation.

The GoFundMe fund-raiser was launched by Kate Jones to help cover Harrison's funeral and memorial costs, as well as household bills and essential expenses while his parents take time away from work to grieve.

By Saturday morning it was nearing its £20,000 target.

"Our family's world was changed forever when Kayleigh and Daryl's beautiful six-year-old son Harrison was tragically hit by a vehicle outside of his own home and sadly passed away at the scene in front of his family," Jones said.

"There are no words that can truly describe the heartbreak and devastation his parents, sisters and our whole family are experiencing," Jones said on the fund-raiser page.

"A child should never be taken from their family so suddenly, under such tragic circumstances and we are all struggling to come to terms with this unimaginable loss," she said.

"Harrison's mum and dad are facing the unimaginable task of saying goodbye to their precious little boy, while trying to somehow navigate life without him so we have set up this fundraiser to help Harrison's parents through the difficult weeks and months ahead."

An investigation into the circumstances of the crash is ongoing and police have asked anyone who witnessed the incident or was in the area around Pen y Bryn Road and Mill Road at the time to get in touch with them.

title: Kim wins Asian Games gold to secure military exemption
content:
Asian Games - final round

-18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chn), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe)

Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.

The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes.

There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see.

South Korean males are, in most circumstances, required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.

However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.

Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.

His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption.

Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.

However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.

title: How airlines try to weed out rogue pilots
content:
Peter Campbell in London

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

A decade after a Germanwings co-pilot crashed a plane into the French Alps, the aviation industry is bound by safety procedures designed to prevent another pilot from going rogue.

Aviation safety regulators across the world tightened rules after that disaster: pilots seeking to enter the profession now face strict psychological tests, along with annual check-ups that include questions about depression and suicide.

Details are still emerging about the assault aboard Flydubai flight 1073 . UAE authorities have said the co-pilot stabbed the pilot with an axe in the cockpit and tried to take control of the plane in a “terrorist act”.

The incident, which follows millions of safe flights over the years, has raised further questions over how the industry monitors pilots’ mental fitness to fly.

Pilots, instructors and safety experts told the FT that current checks may still fail to catch the tiny number of unsuitable people who apply to join the industry, or who develop severe mental health problems or adopt extreme ideological views over a long career.

“It’s effectively self-reporting,” said one commercial pilot. “There are obviously right answers.”

Flying internationally remains a safe form of transport — “the most dangerous part of any flight is always the drive to the airport”, said aviation analyst Andrew Charlton.

But several industry figures argued that this was down to broader safety procedures, stringent pilot training and the professionalism of those in the industry rather than to the psychological testing system.

Pilots must undergo annual check-ups that determine their chances of becoming medically incapacitated during a flight, including a conversation with a doctor about their state of mind, along with questions about alcohol and drug use.

Airlines also carry out regular background checks, which include looking for signs of extremist sympathies.

“We do psychometric testing and background security checks on a regular basis,” said an airline executive.

But one working pilot told the FT their last full psychological analysis was more than two decades ago. Another said pilots “prepare” for their annual check-up and “answer questions to make them think all is well”.

Andrew McKechnie, who spent 30 years as a pilot and now runs McKechnie Aviation, a safety training group, said: “A pilot’s income depends on holding a valid medical certificate, so pilots may be reluctant to seek help for health issues in case they lose their medical certificate . . . Similarly, there’s a strong incentive for pilots to avoid disclosing mental health concerns to their aviation medical examiner.”

However, tightened checks have in some cases helped to identify people whose mental health has deteriorated or who suffer life shocks, pilots said.

Pilots who suffer bereavements or major traumas are required to make several visits to a therapist before returning to flying, said people with knowledge of the process.

After the 2015 Germanwings crash — which killed 150 people and which investigators found had been caused by the deliberate actions of the pilot — most airlines also introduced extensive schemes to enable crew to report colleagues they believe may be unsafe.

This is helpful in an industry where the fluid nature of rosters means that pilots, co-pilots and crew change constantly. Many will have met each other only hours before take-off. “Being able to form a team quickly is part of the job,” said one longtime pilot.

Interventions that follow whistleblowing are robust, helping struggling crew members get help. Multiple people said the system has led to improvements.

It is also open to abuse: the industry is rife with tales of pilots or crew who report each other to the system after the end of a romantic relationship.

The industry’s focus on safety also makes people reluctant to come forward with genuine concerns.

“You cannot declare a problem,” said one person who works in pilot training, adding that people with autism, attention deficit disorder or depression feel unable to speak out. “You can’t get counselling, other than for eating disorders or marriage counselling,” they added.

Working as a pilot entails broken sleep patterns and near-constant jet lag, while long periods away from home can lead to marital strains. One pilot said: “If you’re not OK with your own company — and watching really bad TV in your hotel room — it can be an overwhelming experience.”

But others said they believed changes in the mental state of pilots were more often caused by life events such as divorce than by the job itself. “The most difficult bit is to assess people who have shocks that then trigger and change them into a different personality,” said one former pilot who runs a training centre.

One long-haul airline pilot described the role itself as “pure escapism”. “You see sunshine every day . . . [and] you go to a different part of the world where no one knows who you are,” they said. Another repeated a well-known industry joke: “The pressure is always highest at altitude zero, ie on the ground.”

Flydubai chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith on Friday reiterated that a “full official investigation” was under way into the near miss on its flight, and added: “It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts . . . Safety is, and always will be, our highest priority.” Flydubai declined to comment on pilot checks, pending the investigation.

Investigators have not released the name of the alleged attacker on the flight, though the UAE on Saturday said the flight’s co-pilot “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”.

The co-pilot was “attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft”, UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said. The investigation will “establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident”, he added.

Andrew Lobbenberg, an airline analyst at Barclays, said it “could lead regulators and airlines to revisit psychological screening, crew vetting procedures and access to flight controls when only two pilots are in the cockpit”.

McKechnie is unconvinced by arguments for more testing. He said the checks rely on the belief “that pilots who plan to commit acts of sabotage and murder will discuss this with colleagues, counsellors or medical examiners”.

He added: “These attempts to use psychological and psychiatric assessments to reduce the risk of sabotage by pilots are ineffective.”

But others in the industry disagree. Arik Arad, former security chief of Israeli airline El Al, told CNN this week that pilots “should also have psychological and background checks not only when they get accepted to become pilots but periodically, maybe every six months . . . just to make sure nobody is going astray.”

title: Co-pilot used axe to carry out ‘terrorist act’ on Flydubai flight
content:
Peter Campbell in London

Published October 3 2026

The co-pilot of Flydubai Flight 1073 attacked the captain with an axe in the cockpit as he “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”, UAE prosecutors said on Saturday.

Authorities have been questioning Smit Machchhar, the captain, and his co-pilot, who has not been named, after Wednesday’s incident when a fight on the flight deck broke out in what has been described as an attempted hijacking.

“The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft,” said UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi.

The crash axe is a heavy one-handed axe that sits in the cockpit, allowing pilots to break glass or even punch through bodywork in the event of an emergency.

While it was known that Machchhar had been stabbed, it was unclear until Saturday what weapon had been used. Pilots and crew are subject to the same security checks as passengers.

Al Shamsi added: “Investigations are ongoing to establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, as well as to complete technical examinations and analysis of physical and digital evidence. The final results will be announced upon the conclusion of all necessary procedures.”

Although details of what happened are still emerging, the pilot of the aircraft has been praised for unlocking the cabin door, allowing passengers and crew to enter the cockpit and regain control of the aircraft, which had fallen steeply. The plane, which had been heading for Tel Aviv, was then landed at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia.

Passengers were transferred to Tel Aviv, while Machchhar and the co-pilot were both flown from Saudi Arabia to Abu Dhabi on Thursday “accompanied by the UAE security team”, according to Saudi state media.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”. Israel has not released evidence for that claim.

title: Manchester City’s fightback begins
content:
Josh Noble and Benjamin Wilhelm

Published October 3 2026

This article is an online version of our Scoreboard newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Saturday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

It’s been another gruelling few days for executives at Nike. On Thursday the company announced a fresh round of job cuts and gave investors another gloomy forecast for the year ahead. Shares dropped more than 6 per cent yesterday, their lowest level since 2013.

Sales in China, its second-biggest market, fell by more than a fifth in the first quarter of its financial year ending in August. Nike has been seriously squeezed there by local brands and has so far struggled to regain its footing.

The sportswear maker also announced a new campus in Bengaluru, a sign that it sees India as a potential saviour. But if there’s a light at the end of the tunnel, it’s pretty hard to see right now.

So, time to get on to the biggest story in sport — Manchester City’s legal war against the competition it has come to dominate. Plus, the NFL’s international expansion shows signs of overexposure. Do read on — Josh Noble, sports editor

Send us tips and feedback at [email protected] . Not already receiving the email newsletter? Sign up here . For everyone else, let’s go.

At 7pm on Thursday, Manchester City’s attempts to overturn the damning findings of an independent commission formally kicked off. City was judged to have arranged a series of “sham” sponsorship deals that — along with moves to hide costs off the books — flattered the club’s accounts to the tune of more than £900mn over a period lasting almost a decade.

The club, owned by a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family, said it had lodged its appeal against the Premier League-appointed panel:

The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

The appeal had been widely flagged ahead of time and is just part of the response to the ruling by the club and its allies.

On Wednesday, Abu Dhabi-based airline Etihad threatened legal action against the Premier League, saying its communications around the case had “created damaging implications”. Etihad, City’s principal sponsor, said it “categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements”.

There is a significant political element too. City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak is an influential figure in Abu Dhabi’s government, and chief executive of the sovereign wealth fund Mubadala. You can read our in-depth profile of him here .

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was forced to backtrack on comments earlier this week after saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s owners were forced out. Downing Street later said: “The initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.”

English football’s new independent regulator also weighed in with a rather pointed statement:

The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.

City’s football empire stretches well beyond the Premier League. The parent company has five clubs in Europe alone, with more in Australia, Brazil, the US and beyond. Any suggestion that certain owners or executives are “unsuitable” would have implications across the game.

Legal experts have billed City’s chances of overturning the verdict itself a serious uphill climb. But with the club insisting it will pursue all avenues available, many expect the case to run and run. One lawyer described this week’s events as being more like the “end of the beginning” rather than anything approaching an ending.

This is all pretty miserable for the Premier League. City, after all, are currently top of the league. Bookmakers currently rate the club as the second most likely to be crowned champions and the fourth most likely to be relegated. The uncertainty hanging over the competition will weigh heavily.

In the short term, it’s hard to see much of a knock to the Premier League’s business. If anything, the soap opera may well make the action on the pitch even more enticing for subscription-paying fans.

But if every result against City this season is now going to come with a caveat, the integrity of the world’s most popular football league is going to come under increasing strain.

As the NFL’s footprint spreads around the globe, there are signs of American football fatigue in London, the cradle of the league’s international expansion.

Facing slower ticket sales than usual, the NFL has cut prices down to £79 ($105) for tomorrow’s game between the Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts at Tottenham Stadium. Tickets are available for even less on resale markets.

Excitement was probably damped by initial face-value prices of up to $325 for a match-up of middling teams. The NFL is also playing games in Paris, Madrid and Munich this season, giving fans in Europe options beyond the British capital.

While London remains a hub for the NFL’s global ambitions — it hosts three games this season — the city is just one stop in the league’s ever-growing International Series. This year, that includes a record-breaking nine games spanning seven countries and four continents, with an appetite for more.

The NFL has toyed with the possibility of a Super Bowl in London but more recently backed off the idea. Meanwhile, commissioner Roger Goodell told a German publication last month that he has “no doubt” that there will eventually be an NFL team outside the US.

Such an idea faces significant logistical barriers. A more realistic outcome of the NFL’s global expansion is Goodell’s vision of a 16-game international schedule, which would mean every team plays one game abroad each season. In typical NFL fashion, the league could then carve out a lucrative broadcast rights package to sell to a global streamer like YouTube or Netflix.

The NFL views the Premier League’s global reach as inspiration, as Kansas City Chiefs president Mark Donovan told the FT in June:

It might have been eight years ago now, we sat in a league meeting, and the NFL put up a map of the EPL, and said, “If you look at the EPL, one of the most successful leagues out there, 20 per cent of their franchise fans are in the country. Eighty per cent are around the world. If you look at the NFL, 80 per cent of our fans are in the country, 20 per cent are around the world.”

The league’s efforts to change that include its Global Markets Program, which awards franchises marketing rights to countries to build their own fan bases. The NFL has also invested in the development of flag football around the world, and successfully pushed for the low-contact sport to be added to the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

Time will tell if global audiences embrace American football, a game that mystifies even a few Americans. Last month’s NFL debut in Australia — a San Francisco 49ers blowout of the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne — drew a modest 3.2mn viewers outside the US on Netflix, where it was broadcast globally.

On the other hand, 100,000 fans filled the Melbourne Cricket Ground for that game. Another 72,792 packed Rio de Janeiro’s legendary Maracanã Stadium for last Sunday’s match-up between the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens and erupted when the Ravens won in dramatic fashion .

The NFL played its first game in Brazil just two years ago, compared to the dozens held in London since 2007. The novelty may have faded in the UK but there is still massive room for growth there and beyond.

The board of Madison Square Garden Sports, which owns the NBA’s New York Knicks and the NHL’s New York Rangers, approved the split of the two franchises into separate publicly traded companies.

The NBA is expected to select the winning bid for ownership of a Las Vegas expansion team in the “very near future”, according to ESPN, with a price of at least $12bn to $13bn for the franchise and a new arena.

The US Senate passed legislation that aims to regulate college sports — primarily American football and basketball — which have rapidly professionalised after a series of court rulings allowed revenue sharing and for athletes to profit from their “name, image and likeness”. The bill, which still requires approval from the House of Representatives, would grant the National Collegiate Athletic Association an antitrust exemption to enact rules that cap player pay and limit transfers.

The Chicago White Sox won their first playoff series since 2005 with a sweep of the Houston Astros this week. During the booze-fuelled celebration, Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami sidelined his translator and gave an interview for the ages .
