title: 意大利和希腊寻求欧盟财政规则灵活性
content:
意大利和希腊本周分别致信欧盟委员会，请求在欧盟财政规则下获得更多财政回旋空间。伊朗战争导致柴油和汽油价格上涨，推高两国燃料价格支持措施成本，加剧公共财政压力。两国均将于明年举行选举。
意大利总理焦尔吉娅·梅洛尼和希腊总理基里亚科斯·米佐塔基斯分别致信欧盟委员会，请求在欧盟财政规则下获得更大操作空间。欧盟财政规则要求成员国年度赤字不超过国内生产总值的3%。欧盟财政规则已于6月调整，临时允许各国在2028年前将相当于国内生产总值0.6%的资金用于减少对进口化石燃料依赖的能源投资。这是更广泛豁免的一部分，允许各国将相当于国内生产总值1.5%的资金用于国防和能源，意大利和希腊均在利用该豁免，且不会因此受到惩罚性措施。
本周的新请求更进一步。希腊请求允许将“临时措施”排除在其净支出指标之外，分析人士称这指的是燃料补贴。意大利请求在评估其预算是否符合欧盟支出上限时考虑通胀因素。欧盟官员私下警告，在财政规则下给予额外灵活性可能引发市场负面反应。
梅洛尼周四致信欧盟委员会主席乌尔苏拉·冯德莱恩，要求在下周欧盟财政部长会议上讨论此事。她在信中指出，意大利应被允许将因通胀征收的额外税收用于减轻家庭和企业面临的价格上涨影响，而不违反财政规则。她写道，部分额外收入应“以临时和有针对性的方式用于抑制能源成本上升”。信中还呼吁布鲁塞尔在意大利2027年预算预测超过欧盟年度支出阈值时，将通胀视为缓解因素。
意大利财政部长贾恩卡洛·焦尔杰蒂周五晚公布意大利新财政规划文件，预计今年财政赤字将降至国内生产总值的3%以下，经济增长将达到1%，高于4月预测的0.6%。但焦尔杰蒂表示，意大利2027年赤字将升至国内生产总值的3.4%，因意大利启动所谓国家免责条款，请求欧盟为明年和2028年额外能源和国防支出提供相当于国内生产总值0.6%的额外空间，两年共计290亿欧元额外资源，前提是议会同意。2028年赤字将降至3.2%，仍利用欧盟额外灵活性，2029年降至2.3%。2027年至2029年经济增长将保持在1%以下，介于0.8%至0.9%之间。意大利公共债务预计明年达到国内生产总值的138.5%峰值，届时将取代希腊成为欧盟负债最重经济体，随后逐步下降。
焦尔杰蒂确认，鉴于其所称“特别复杂”的经济环境，意大利决定未来两年国防支出低于此前考虑。自2022年执政以来，梅洛尼联盟因财政审慎和克制赢得债务投资者和信用评级机构赞誉，将意大利财政赤字从2022年的8%降至2025年的3.1%。但罗马今年在燃料消费税削减上支出约28亿欧元。上周，意大利国家控制的能源集团埃尼表示将对加油站价格实施临时价格上限，至少持续一个月，以支持政府努力。
米佐塔基斯也向布鲁塞尔请求更大灵活性，在周三致冯德莱恩的信中呼吁更多“喘息空间”。他提议允许成员国利用价格上涨产生的额外税收收入，为保护家庭和企业免受能源成本上升影响的临时支持措施提供资金。他还批评欧盟委员会关于减少能源需求的建议“在政治上不可接受”。此举正值生活成本成为米佐塔基斯政府关键关切，希腊将于明年春季举行全国选举。欧盟委员会拒绝置评。

title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
content:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.

Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.

The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.

The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.

The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.

He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"

The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."

He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".

The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.

He also said investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.

Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.

"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.

About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply.

The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.

In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.

Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."

People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit.

Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries.

Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".

Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.

He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.

In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

title: 日本最大自动售货机制造商富士电机将制冷技术转用于数据中心冷却
content:
日本最大自动售货机制造商富士电机利用其制冷技术，为耗电量巨大的人工智能数据中心开发出节能冷却系统，据称可降低能耗85%。该技术原本用于冷却碳酸饮料、茶和咖啡，标志着日本工业集团竞相转型为人工智能基础设施关键组件供应商的最新动向。
富士电机生产日本80%的自动售货机。该公司将原本用于自动售货机的制冷技术重新设计，推出数据中心冷却系统。冷却服务器占数据中心能耗的30%至40%，为擅长空调和制冷技术的日本企业提供了巨大机遇。富士电机此举加入 松下 、三菱电机和住友电气等日本工业集团的行列，这些企业正将自身重新定位为人工智能基础设施关键组件供应商。
富士电机的技术源于2011年福岛核事故后提高自动售货机能效的努力。当时自动售货机成为浪费能源的象征，时任东京都知事石原慎太郎曾要求全面关闭自动售货机以节省电力。这一呼吁促使富士电机和丰田供应商 电装 开发新型冷却系统。2015年，研究团队利用二氧化碳制冷剂开发出喷射器，无需压缩机，节能20%。富士电机负责向数据中心推销该技术的白井秀人表示：“仅仅扩展现有技术是不够的。”
多数冷却系统使用压缩机，耗大量电力将制冷剂转化为高温高压气体。富士电机的喷射器利用废热驱动制冷剂通过精密设计的喷嘴，通过流体运动提高压力。然而该技术从未在自动售货机中采用，因为安装成本过高，而自动售货机本身仅值数千美元。白井表示：“我们知道这项技术有效。”“但很难让它在自动售货机中开花结果。于是想法开始形成：如果我们将其应用于另一个工业领域呢？”
这家总部位于东京的电气设备供应商计划到2030年向数据中心销售超过100亿日元（约6100万美元）的喷射器系统。该公司已每年销售1000亿日元的数据中心相关组件，如开关设备。作为人工智能“卖铲人”供应商的角色，以及能源组件业务利润率改善，推动富士电机股价过去一年上涨近47%，公司估值达139亿美元。
数据基础设施研究机构Dell‘Oro研究总监亚历克斯·科多维尔称该技术“有前景”，但仍“真正处于新兴阶段”。数据中心冷却市场正从使用水和乙二醇或氢氟烯烃制冷剂的传统系统，转向直接液体冷却，即将液体冷却剂直接循环至CPU和GPU等发热组件。富士电机的系统可用于直接液体冷却系统。喷射器技术在日本夏季气温常超35度的部分地区以及东南亚等高温地区表现更佳。但科多维尔表示，利用废热的竞争技术——日本川崎、荏原和矢崎制造的吸收式冷水机组——在数据中心应用方面比富士系统更具优势。
高盛 分析师原田亮对富士电机能否进入美国大型数据中心市场表示怀疑。他说：“技术可能引人注目，但商业化同样重要。”“超大规模企业已在很大程度上锁定未来两到三年的下一代数据中心架构，因此新进入者可能需要至少同样长时间才能获得有意义的进展。”

title: 私募资本大举投资欧洲青年旅舍市场
content:
过去18个月，博枫、阿波罗等全球私募资本巨头对欧洲青年旅舍行业进行重大投资，推动这一长期被机构投资者忽视的旅游细分领域走向标准化和高端化。该行业增长速度快于主流酒店，引发市场关注。
博枫资产管理规模约1万亿美元，去年以7.76亿欧元收购总部位于伦敦的Generator Hostels欧洲业务。此前，房地产私募股权公司L&G Proprium于2023年收购另一欧洲连锁品牌A&O Hostels，A&O于今年4月从阿波罗获得8.74亿欧元融资。A&O和Generator均计划将规模扩大一倍。仲量联行房地产顾问公司副总裁安德鲁·希思表示，青年旅舍是“住宿行业中最后一个尚未真正被机构投资者触及的领域”。“人们正在观察并思考：青年旅舍能否被机构化？能否实现标准化和高端化？”
市场数据显示，截至今年8月的12个月内，欧洲大型青年旅舍——即可容纳超过100名客人的旅舍——数量增长13%至83家。尽管总数仍然较小，但增速超过酒店和其他类型住宿。博枫董事总经理劳伦·冈田·扬表示，机构投资者目前正“围绕这一市场，并看到其经济模式相当有利可图和具有吸引力”。她指出，博枫被青年旅舍行业吸引，是因为其扩张空间远大于酒店市场。
Generator的“高端旅舍”旨在保持低成本的同时，增加现代设计和配套设施，包括屋顶露台和全方位服务咖啡馆等通常与精品酒店相关的元素。L&G Proprium联合管理合伙人菲利普·韦斯特曼表示：“该行业非常分散，因此在此搭建平台并实现规模化的能力很有意思。”他补充说，青年旅舍通常不提供客房服务，因此人员成本可低于酒店，而经济型定价使其在经济动荡中更具韧性。
博枫旗下Generator计划到2030年将欧洲资产翻倍至30家旅舍。首席执行官泽维尔·穆弗拉吉表示，他正在寻找至少可容纳500张床位的物业，因为该模式依赖高入住率，只有在“临界规模”下才能成功。穆弗拉吉指出，Z世代是主要增长市场，因为他们“希望更多旅行，但收入低于前辈”。A&O在欧洲拥有40多家旅舍，计划未来五年将资产组合翻倍。该公司正投资4000万欧元将柏林市中心一栋前办公楼改造为拥有2500张床位的旅舍，预计2027年年中开业，届时将成为欧洲最大旅舍。
近年来，闲置办公楼成为欧洲青年旅舍行业的增长来源。A&O首席执行官奥利弗·温特表示，将大型办公楼改造为酒店具有挑战性，因为需要将大空间分割为带独立管道和自然光的单独房间，但青年旅舍宿舍大小可变且客户要求较低，更适合这种改造。穆弗拉吉表示，该行业目前最大的房地产机会在于陷入困境的中档酒店，这些酒店通常能为旅舍运营商带来更好回报。
大众旅游公司也在进军青年旅舍领域。英国旅游运营商Jet2于2025年推出首批以青年旅舍为基础的度假套餐，以吸引更年轻和价格敏感的客户。部分人士担心，私募股权支持的“连锁旅舍”增长将削弱历史悠久、风格简朴的旅舍魅力。旅游平台StayAltered创始人埃文·曾表示：“你所妥协的是许多旅行者喜爱的本地真实氛围。”

title: 纽约一写字楼租金创纪录 对冲基金Castle Hook年付最高2120万美元
content:
纽约曼哈顿中城一座摩天大楼近日创下写字楼租金纪录，低调对冲基金Castle Hook Partners租下其顶层两层，年租金最高达2120万美元。
Castle Hook Partners将于2029年下半年入驻房地产开发商Related Companies拥有的麦迪逊大道625号办公大楼顶层。据知情人士透露，该基金愿意为5.3万平方英尺空间支付每平方英尺每年350至400美元租金，显示曼哈顿高端写字楼市场繁荣正在加速。此前写字楼租金纪录于今年早些时候创下，一家国际私人家族办公室在Soloviev Group拥有的中城大楼签署10年租约，平均每平方英尺327.50美元。
Related首席执行官杰夫·布劳在接受采访时表示，该公司原计划在该地块建造豪华高层住宅，该地块于2024年初从SL Green购得，但最终决定利用“全新、配套完善、高端且拥有绝佳景观的写字楼”所存在的“真正溢价”。这座53层高楼俯瞰中央公园，由英国建筑师诺曼·福斯特勋爵设计，顶层和“配套设施层”将设有私人餐饮设施和环绕式露台。布劳表示，金融服务和科技行业的人才争夺战，加上吸引员工重返办公室的努力，造就了纽约豪华写字楼的黄金时代。
Castle Hook由戴维·罗杰斯于2016年创立，目前总部位于第五大道 通用汽车 大楼。该公司早期投资者包括传奇对冲基金经理斯坦利·德鲁肯米勒，在华尔街保持低调。根据其最新监管文件，该公司管理约110亿美元资产，拥有35名员工。该公司属于所谓全球宏观对冲基金，交易外汇、大宗商品、债券和股票中的宏观经济趋势。研究机构PivotalPath数据显示，截至8月底，宏观基金今年上涨6.8%。Castle Hook近年来回报较高，据报道去年上涨约50%，前年上涨超过60%。Castle Hook发言人未回应置评请求。
对冲基金之间的人才争夺日趋激烈，豪华办公室和配套设施正成为除高薪之外争夺顶级投资组合经理的方式。对冲基金和其他金融公司是疫情后首批要求员工重返办公室的公司之一。知名对冲基金经理比尔·阿克曼和丹·勒布等人曾强烈批评纽约市长佐赫兰·马姆达尼的民粹政策及其对纽约房地产市场的潜在影响。马姆达尼赢得民主党初选后，一些华尔街高管私下警告其崛起将促使金融公司迁出纽约。布劳表示：“人们可能对纽约政治有自己的看法，但我认为人们相信纽约市的未来。”Related执行副总裁斯蒂芬·温特表示，麦迪逊大道大楼到年底将出租67%，主要租户为金融服务公司。私募股权公司General Atlantic将租用五层作为主力租户。 摩根大通 2025年揭幕的总部设有最先进的健康中心和19种餐饮选择，为纽约各地新写字楼配套设施设定了基调。

title: 美国银行团体起诉货币监理署 指控其越权向加密公司发放信托牌照
content:
美国独立社区银行家协会（ICBA）周五在联邦法院起诉美国货币监理署（OCC），指控该监管机构越权向加密公司发放国家信托银行牌照，使其在未受到与社区银行同等监管的情况下进入 美国银行 体系，导致小型银行面临严重竞争劣势。
ICBA是美国最大银行业倡导组织之一，通常代表较小机构。该组织上月曾在阻止《数字资产市场清晰法案》推进方面发挥重要作用，部分原因是其反对该法案稳定币条款未能保护社区银行免受存款账户直接竞争。此次诉讼针对加密公司寻求的信托牌照，该牌照正被用作进入美国银行和支付体系的入口。
ICBA总裁兼首席执行官丽贝卡·罗梅罗·雷尼在声明中表示：“国会设立国家信托牌照，并不是为寻求联邦银行牌照信誉的加密公司打开进入银行体系的侧门。”她指出，这些公司无需承担资本、流动性、监管以及联邦存款保险公司保险要求等同等义务。美国货币监理署发言人回应称，该机构“不对诉讼置评”。
货币监理署持续向加密公司发放信托牌照，但这些公司运营模式与典型社区银行不同，不提供联邦存款保险公司保险所针对和要求的现金存款账户。银行政策研究所执行副总裁兼监管事务联席主管佩奇·皮达诺·帕里东在文章发表后表示，该机构支持将创新产品和服务引入受监管银行生态系统，前提是从事实类活动的实体须遵守与其他持牌机构相同的规则和责任。她指出，公司除非仅从事“信托活动”，否则不应获得信托牌照；“如果它们想从事传统银行活动，应寻求全方位银行牌照。严格、统一的标准对于培育竞争、安全和有韧性的银行体系至关重要。”
银行业监管机构曾将行业寻求国家信托牌照视为在长期空白后新银行名称的复苏。部分信托机构以加密专注银行形式成立，如Protego和Erebor；其他则来自现有知名加密企业，如Coinbase、 Circle 和Crypto.com。近期新增World Liberty Financial，该公司由美国总统特朗普及其家族部分持有，其牌照获批引发包括民主党参议员伊丽莎白·沃伦在内的批评者不满。沃伦指责该机构允许总统腐败，并在社交媒体上发文称新牌照“给他及其家族提供了新的获利途径”。上月，货币监理署还向OpenReserve Bank发放了正式国家银行牌照，该区块链银行由Andreessen Horowitz、Jump Capital和Coinbase Ventures等多家加密投资者资助。

title: 美国9月就业发布后比特币24小时内上涨超过2%
content:
美国劳工部周五公布的非农就业报告显示，美国9月新增就业2.9万人，远低于市场预期的9万人；8月新增就业数据从16.2万下修至13.3万；7月新增就业从2.1万下修为减少1万。9月失业率升至4.2%，高于预期的4.1%和8月的4.1%。报告表明美国劳动力市场走弱，可能为美联储在通胀仍处高位情况下维持利率提供空间。
薪资增长同样低于预期。9月平均时薪环比上涨0.1%，低于预期的0.3%和8月的0.3%；同比上涨3%，低于预期的3.2%和8月的3.1%。
数据公布后，金融市场反应明显。比特币保持此前涨幅，24小时内上涨超过2%，略低于8.7万美元。美国股指期货扩大涨幅， 纳斯达克 指数上涨1.2%。10年期美国国债收益率下跌7个基点至5.17%，2年期美国国债收益率下跌类似幅度至4.71%。黄金上涨超过1%，美元对主要货币下跌。

title: 特朗普拟任命克莱顿为人工智能事务负责人
content:
据报道，美国总统特朗普可能任命前美国证券交易委员会主席杰伊·克莱顿为政府人工智能事务负责人。克莱顿在担任证交会主席期间主导了对加密货币行业的执法打击，其过往记录可能引发人工智能行业关注。
克莱顿曾在特朗普首个任期内担任证交会主席，此前任纽约南区联邦检察官，今年被任命为特朗普的国家情报总监。据悉，他即将出任的人工智能事务负责人一职将聚焦政府“人工智能力量”项目，负责监管快速增长的国内人工智能产业。该职位议程似乎不包括加密货币，尽管两个领域存在重大重叠。特朗普首任加密货币和人工智能事务负责人戴维·萨克斯已于今年3月离任，白宫加密货币事务此后由顾问帕特里克·维特负责。
克莱顿在证交会任职期间，于2017年设立证交会“网络部门”，开始监管首次代币发行及其他行业活动。到2020年离任时，该机构发布报告概述其执法记录，包括针对数字资产、区块链企业和首次代币发行提起的57起案件。证交会称，这些案件聚焦“通过使用数字资产证券欺诈投资者的行为，以及在数字资产证券要约和销售中违反联邦证券法注册条款的行为”。克莱顿在2020年即将离任时，启动了证交会对瑞波实验室的高调法律诉讼，指控其未将约13亿美元的XRP代币注册为证券。该案后来被特朗普任命的现任证交会主席保罗·阿特金斯终止，证交会去年放弃进一步追诉。
克莱顿的执法立场为后来加里·根斯勒领导证交会期间的“以执法促监管”加密政策奠定了基础。根斯勒是前总统乔·拜登任命的民主党人。特朗普在首个任期内曾对加密货币持怀疑态度。他在2021年接受采访时谈及“世界上的比特币”时表示：“我认为他们应该非常、非常严格地监管它们。”特朗普此后转向支持数字资产，从首次涉足非同质化代币到推出个人迷因币并入股World Liberty Financial。他在2024年竞选期间重新塑造为加密货币支持者，重返白宫后聘请萨克斯同时监管加密货币和人工智能政策。
特朗普9月在社交平台上宣布人工智能力量项目时，将其比作首个任期内创建的太空军，并表示将在“不久的将来”宣布人工智能事务负责人，称此人将是一位“高智商”人士。克莱顿在重返公共部门担任联邦检察官前，曾在私募股权巨头阿波罗全球管理公司董事会任职数年，该公司投入数十亿美元支持人工智能和数字基础设施项目。克莱顿近期在接受采访时表示，他将人工智能视为国家安全问题，但拒绝讨论暂停该技术发展的提议。他说：“我不认为任何美国人应该认为那是一个好战略。”

title: Film festival celebrates British-Latino identity
content:
An event billed as London's only competitive Latino film festival is now under way for the first time in the capital.

Venues including the Barbican, the ICA, Ciné Lumière and BFI Stephen Street will screen 60 films from 27 countries until Tuesday.

There will also be workshops and performances with guests including Cuban dancer Carlos Acosta, a former principal at the Royal Ballet, Argentine actor Óscar Martínez, Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Oscar-winning Chilean screenwriter Gonzalo Maza.

The event was founded by Cuban actress Ketty Rodriguez who, when she moved to London, was struck by the lack of Latin representation in a city famous for its multiculturalism, film and history.

She told BBC London: "Everything here is about community, is about connection, and the idea started because I couldn't find my people, I didn't know where they were, so I decided to do this festival and it's very successful, I'm very happy."

Rodriguez says it is the first competitive Latino film festival of this size in London.

"We have received hundreds of entries from all over Latin America, and can't wait to support and showcase features, documentaries, animation, and shorts from these incredible filmmakers," she said.

Cuban dancer Javier Torres, who developed the festival idea with Rodriguez, said: "This is just the start of something great. We found a gap in the market, we found a necessity of the Latino community to come together and to give voice and narrative voices to Latin American filmmakers.

"This is a platform for diplomacy, for culture, to get together and this is what we are building here."

Alongside entries from Latin America are stories made in London for Londoners.

Victor Rios, a British-Bolivian filmmaker said the event was a chance "not just to celebrate people of Latin roots but also to celebrate British-Latino identity".

He moved to the UK at 16, and has two short films in the selection.

He said: "It's very crucial for people to understand that we are not just here passing by. We are part of society, and this festival is establishing that too.

"We're very proud to be Colombians, Bolivians, Ecuadorians, Peruvians, Chileans, but we are also British.

"So we have a place, we have a say, and we want to be heard."

The festival is backed by the BFI through National Lottery funding and by the City of London Corporation.

title: Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
content:
Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek.

Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain.

The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint.

On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title.

"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport.

"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality."

Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China.

She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter.

Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent.

Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury.

"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong.

Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title.

Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way.

"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong.

"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense."

The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025.

The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023.

Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China.

If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili.

"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong.

The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira.

When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response.

"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

title: Island hosts inter-island environment summit
content:
Environmental experts, conservation groups and businesses from across the British Isles and France have gathered in Guernsey for the 26th Inter-Island Environment Meeting.

The annual event, co-ordinated by the Guernsey Nature Commission, brings together delegates to share ideas and develop joint projects aimed at protecting the natural environment.

This year's theme, Nature for the Next Generation, includes talks on subjects ranging from seabird restoration and woodland resilience to butterfly monitoring in Sark and citizen science projects.

A Sixth Form Environment Meeting gave young people the chance to present environmental issues that matter to them and contribute ideas for the future.

Students will take part in workshops linked to Guernsey's upcoming Marine Spatial Plan, helping shape discussions about the future protection and management of the island's seas.

Angela Salmon, head of education at the Nature Commission and a member of the meeting group said inviting sixth formers to share the environmental issues that mattered to them "makes perfect sense".

Among those attending was Sebastian Dufour, an independent consultant for the Alderney Wildlife Trust, who joined a field trip to Lihou Island exploring its ecology and archaeology.

He said he had learned about a Benedictine Priory site "which is very interesting" and discovered there had been "a really remarkably large industry in harvesting seaweed".

Dufour said he particularly valued the collaborative nature of the event, adding: "We're all coming from different islands and we're all facing similar challenges."

He said the annual meeting provided an opportunity to "learn from each other" and "share our successes and failures and everything".

title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
content:
A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.

The attack on Saturday morning injured two people, and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic jams.

It comes after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart".

Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.

The Russian strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the wide river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day - though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level.

Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city every day. The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two.

Writing on Telegram on Saturday morning, Klitschko said "emergency services are on their way" after the Pivnichnyi Bridge was hit.

"Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added.

Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.

Klitschko warned afterwards that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

More powerful weapons could collapse the bridges, some of which are reported to be in poor condition after years carrying heavier traffic than they were designed for.

It was reported that Ukrainian lawmakers discussed the state of Kyiv's bridges in a recent meeting, setting out contingency plans to use ferries or temporary pontoon bridges to keep the city connected in the event of any bridges being destroyed.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

After the Pivdennyi Bridge was attacked, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.

In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings."

He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."

Putin on Thursday insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.

"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.

The Kremlin leader admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.

In other developments on Saturday:

A sailor on a Liberia-flagged civilian ship was killed and another three crew members injured in a Russian attack on Ukraine's Black Sea port in the Odesa region, the Ukrainian port authorities said

At least 12 people were injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and Kyiv regions, local officials said

Two people were killed and three injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in the country's eastern Luhansk region occupied by Russia, the Moscow-installed regional head said

title: 'I watched 800 films in Covid, now I direct them'
content:
During the coronavirus lockdown in 2020, Benjamin Williams, a lifelong film fan, watched 800 films.

"I just found the time. Plus, it was Covid - I was bored," said the now 28-year-old, looking back.

He started out with dreams of becoming an animator, inspired by films like Avatar: The Last Airbender and Pokemon, before going on to study film at Hereford Sixth Form College, which "opened a whole world" for him.

Williams, from Malvern, has now directed his own film and worked with the likes of Marvel and, most recently, was an assistant director on Apple TV's hit series, Slow Horses, starring award-winners Sir Gary Oldman and Dame Kristin Scott Thomas.

"I have signed many NDAs [non-disclosure agreements] over the years, and obviously, Slow Horses has been one of them.

"I can't say anything about it - obviously the cast and crew are amazing - it's a very wonderful show to work on.

"That's probably the one I've learnt the most on, because that's the one I've spent the most amount of time on," he said.

The spy thriller series is based on the best-selling novel Slow Horses by Mick Herron and premiered in 2022, with a seventh season set for release in 2027.

Oldman stars as the crude boss of a team of failed or disgraced MI5 agents who have been banished to a building called Slough House.

"I worked in the production department, which is logistics, all sorts of paperwork and call sheets, and you manage all of the schedules - that's a very heavy admin-based role," said Williams.

"I actually have worked on the floor for a couple of days because I'm also an AD [assistant director] as well... which I love doing."

He describes Oldman as the biggest star he has worked with.

"That is a pinch-me moment every time you see him," he said.

"He is pretty cool. He's a pretty cool dude."

He also worked on Marvel's VisionQuest, which releases later this year.

"I did a lovely film, only a week on it just for additional photography, called The Christophers, with Sir Ian McKellen, who I was very fortunate just to briefly meet," he said.

"There's such an incredible aura around him of just, 'Oh god, it's Ian McKellen'."

He has also worked on Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan with John Krasinski, the Squid Games reality show and the Peaky Blinders film, Immortal Man.

"I did get to meet Cillian, but again, very similar to Ian, I was just like, 'Hi, cool, move on, great', which was really fun."

His own short film, Keys, premiered at the Worcester Film Festival in September and has been nominated for "best local film" at the Birmingham Film Festival.

'Good impression'

Williams said making a good impression in the industry and working hard had helped his journey.

"As long as you do a good job, you show up, and you're likeable enough, people want to continue working with you, which is how I landed Slow Horses while I was working on a Marvel show," he said.

"I got an email from a lovely coordinator... I think they just did the new The Thomas Crown Affair film with Michael B Jordan.

"He just sort of reached out because I'd been recommended... they were like, 'We heard you did a great job on this; could you come and do this or this?'"

He added: "I have been lucky, but also at the same time, I think I'm honest enough to know that I can back myself and that I've worked hard to get to those positions as well."

title: Victorian bridge hidden under reservoir is revealed
content:
Months of dry weather and prolonged heat have revealed a bridge dating back to Victorian times that had been submerged during the creation of a reservoir.

The old stone Bessom Bridge flooded nearly 50 years ago when Wimbleball Reservoir was created at Exmoor National Park in Somerset. It was later replaced by a new bridge.

In the summer, the Environment Agency declared that Wimbleball was one of the top three lowest reservoirs in the country after levels were recorded as "exceptionally low".

Dr Lucy Shipley, historic environment record officer for Exmoor, said: "We live in an ever-changing world and it's not a kind of fixed point where things stay the same."

Shipley said there were other archaeological finds beneath the lake which were not demolished before the reservoir were created, including a barrow dating back to the Bronze Age.

It is not known why some structures were demolished and others were not.

The former Bessom Bridge used to cross a stream that fed into the River Haddeo, while the new one crosses the north side of the lake.

When water levels drop, the old bridge can be seen from the new one.

Shipley said the changing landscape on Exmoor was "extraordinary".

"The photographs are incredible, they're just so dramatic of the bridge poking out from the silt and sediment that's covered it.

"We live in an ever-changing world and it's not a kind of fixed point where things stay the same, but then by contrast… there's been a consistency of settlement and people living in farming and working in similar ways, so it's that balance of understanding how the world around us is always changing and responding, but also recognising that some things are really consistent over time."

She added that the historic bridge could be enjoyed from afar and asked visitors to refrain from walking on the dried-up section of the reservoir.

Elsewhere around the county, traces of centuries-old gardens were found in Bishop's Palace in Wells, while relics of old structures were uncovered at Glastonbury Abbey due to the record-breaking summer temperatures.

Wimbeball Reservoir, which supplies water to hundreds of thousands of homes across the South West, has a capacity of 21,320 megalitres - one megalitre is a million litres.

The reservoir remains low following record-breaking temperatures over the summer, with a current capacity of only 21.1% as of 27 September, according to South West Water.

Hundreds of thousands of people remain under hosepipe bans across the country while water sources recover from the prolonged dry weather.

The National Drought Group said the recent rain has not been enough to replenish supplies, with drought only being over when rivers, groundwater and reservoirs return to normal levels.

Research from the Environment Agency showed the country will need 120% of typical rainfall over the next seven months for all areas to be considered out of drought.

title: New baby bank 'open to everybody'
content:
The lead volunteer of a new baby bank, which gives away free children's products to those in need, says it is "open to everybody".

The Newent hub of Forest of Dean Baby Bank at The Ark Cafe in Newent, Gloucestershire, offers everything from baby wipes and breast pumps to hats and swimwear, and can also source larger items like cots from a warehouse in Cinderford.

Helen Carter, lead volunteer, says no one will be means tested, with parents often picking up new items while donating what no longer fits their child.

Kylie, a Newent mum visiting the baby bank, said: "It's always expensive to buy new baby things and food and nappies and wipes. So to have the support locally is wonderful."

A lot of the items available at the faciltity are donated, which Carter said the team was "really, really grateful for".

Currently, autumn clothing bundles are in demand, but volunteers have already started putting together a Christmas box of festive clothing, blankets, and shoes.

"A lot of people say, 'I don't need it, I'm okay', but then a lot of people are just sort of managing their finances and are unable to have a nice day out with their children," Carter said.

"But if they [visit the baby bank], then they would be able to pay for that day out, so they might not think they're struggling, but it helps."

In its latest Parent Experience Report, The National Childbirth Trust said nearly half of parents said they were struggling more financially after having a baby, a figure which rose to about six in ten among self-employed, unemployed or part-time employed parents.

Kylie, who was on her first visit to the bank, said clothing and supplies for children were "always expensive".

"I'm quite lucky, I do have an older child as well, so I've got a lot of hand-me-downs," she said.

"But for everyone who hasn't got an older child and [do] formula feeding and things like that, it is very expensive to keep them clean and fed."

Volunteer Isabel said she wanted to give back to the centre after she was helped with food parcels and clothing.

"I know from having three small children that there is a massive need in the area, so I think this is a great thing that we're doing here," she said.

"I just wish more people knew about it."

The baby bank is open every Tuesday morning from 09.30 to 11.30.

title: Man desperate to find teen he saved 30 years ago
content:
A man who risked his own life to rescue a stranger from drowning 30 years ago is trying to track him down.

Lee Heyes jumped into a quarry when he was 15 after he realised the older teen had got into difficulty.

The now 45-year-old, from Chorley, who has written a song about the ordeal, said instinct took over when the stranger, who he thinks was about 18 or 19, jumped in the water at Eccleston Delph and disappeared under the surface after getting tangled in reeds.

"It has really bothered me ever since," he said. "I would love to know how he is getting on."

Lee, who is a plasterer and singer songwriter, performing as "soundstruggles", recalls there being all sorts in the water - even cars at the bottom - when the incident happened in the mid 90s.

He said it took him three attempts, diving deep under the surface, to find the teenager.

After managing to untangle him, Lee said it was a struggle to get him back to the surface as he was "much bigger than me".

Lee got his friends to enter the water to help keep the teenager's head above the surface while he swam to get help from a dad who was in a dinghy with his son.

By this point, Lee recalls being shattered but said the adrenaline spurred him on to raise the alarm. The dad then used the dinghy to get the teenager ashore.

Lee said the stranger walked off afterwards without saying a word. "I presume he was in shock," he added.

He said looking back it could have been a very different outcome.

"I could easily have died myself that day," he said.

Lee's message to anyone thinking of swimming in open water is "don't do it because it is so dangerous".

The trauma of that fateful day has never gone away and Lee believes it triggered anxiety.

Lee, who is one of the stars at this weekend's Chorley Live which features 280 performances across 36 venues in the town and has more than 10,000 followers on TikTok, has written a song about the ordeal called Aqualung.

The moving song has helped him deal with what happened, he said.

"It is a long time to carry that burden."

He said the teenager had blond hair and was about 5ft 10in (1.78m). He was wearing a Liverpool FC shirt and was with two girls.

Lee added: "I would love to know how he is getting on so if he or one of the girls was with him, could contact me that would be amazing."

title: How rapist priest exploited charisma to abuse his 'cult-like' congregation
content:
In the detailed written instructions given to the young women who worked without pay in the then-Reverend Chris Brain's house, there was a revealing demand.

The homebase team, as they were known, were to "do anything" the Church of England priest asked of them.

Routine tasks - assigned on a rota 24 hours a day, seven days a week - included cooking, cleaning, ironing, shopping, looking after Brain's young daughter, and walking his dog.

This housework was intended to free Brain for his mission of leading the Nine O'Clock Service (NOS), a radical congregation of hundreds of young people drawn weekly to a Sheffield church in the 1980s and 1990s by a fusion of rave culture, live music, environmental activism and liturgy.

But the lengthy list of homebase team duties did not spell out other demands Brain made in the attic bedroom of his family's end-terrace house in the suburb of Crookes, heard jurors at his retrial on charges of rape and indecent assault.

On Friday at Inner London Crown Court, the 69-year-old was found guilty of raping one woman in his congregation and four indecent assaults against three others.

He had already been convicted of 17 indecent assaults in August 2025 but faced a retrial as jurors could not reach verdicts on five further counts.

Brain will be sentenced later this year and has been told he is facing a custodial term.

His sentencing will conclude a dramatic and protracted downfall for a preacher who at one point had been preparing to take NOS global with expansion to the US.

The charismatic and domineering preacher, seen by many followers as a prophet, would routinely summon members of his congregation to "put him to bed" with sensual massages, jurors heard.

Often Brain would strip to his underwear and expect kissing and sexual touching with the women, who feared being ostracised - or even damned - if they refused, the court heard.

"By displeasing Brain, you were displeasing God," explained one woman, who gave evidence last month during her former vicar's sexual assault trial.

The movement took root in the early 1980s when Brain, his wife Lynne and small group of like-minded Christian friends joined St Thomas's church in Crookes.

These dozen or so new worshippers - clustered around a band called Present Tense - were devout but disillusioned with traditional Anglican worship. Brain, their bassist and de facto leader, railed against "fancy golf club Christianity" which did not connect with them culturally.

In 1984, the church's vicar Robert Warren gave the group an opportunity to run their own experimental service, every Sunday at 21:00.

The band - who had played gigs across the north of England and performed before U2 at the Christian festival Greenbelt - ditched their evangelical rock songs in favour of a new sound influenced by Sheffield's burgeoning electronic music scene.

NOS was a sensation - attracting a youthful congregation of up to 600 people with an innovative blend of cutting-edge music, video, prayer, and dancing.

"It's the most entertaining church I've been to. It's the best dance night in Sheffield," one worshipper told a 1990 BBC Radio 4 programme, which reported how NOS was "bridging the gap between the church and the people".

One NOS member put it more bluntly in a TV documentary five years later: "We were sticking two fingers up to normal, middle-class church ways of behaviour."

The Diocese of Sheffield, thrilled by the sight of students queueing down the road to worship to the pulsing sound of house music, fast-tracked Brain's route to priesthood despite the reservations of his ordination tutor. The Archbishop of Canterbury told Brain he would be happy to see a NOS in every town and city in Britain.

The services, which later moved to a larger space at Ponds Forge leisure centre, were a huge production involving a crew of up to 150 volunteers - among them musicians, sound technicians, designers, security, and a trucking team. A new multimedia service was planned each week, with volunteers working unpaid throughout Sunday into the early hours of Monday morning to pull it off.

Warren, who had oversight of NOS in its first years at St Thomas's, told the court he initially believed Brain's"controlling" nature helped to get things done.

But as the popularity of NOS grew, the vicar noticed "cult-like elements" emerging. Brain's congregation seemed to look at him "almost as a guru," Warren said in evidence at Brain's first trial.

NOS members were expected to live simply and pay at least 10% of their income to the tight-knit and passionate community, though the court heard many gave more. Some handed over their inheritances and even houses.

Brain, meanwhile, had a modern car, a mobile phone, designer clothes and went on expensive holidays. In 1994, he moved his family to live in a renovated Peak District farmhouse which had been donated to NOS, jurors heard.

"He seemed to be living a luxurious lifestyle when other people are scrimping and scraping along," one NOS member told the court.

Another, who estimated she had given £40,000 to NOS over seven years, recalled the "manipulative" Brain persuading her to skip her brother's wedding in South Africa and buy a van for the community instead.

NOS members told the court they were expected to cut ties with family and friends outside the community.

Jurors were told that one woman was reprimanded by Brain and other NOS leaders for going home to see her family on a weekend: "There were messages to the point of, 'This is your family now. Sacrifice now, for the greater good'."

Women gave evidence that Brain would "groom" them by pulling up to them on the street in his car and inviting them for a drive. On some occasions during this "Chris-napping" - as it was known in the community - he would touch the women and berate them for being sexually repressed, both trials were told.

One victim recalled: "He grabbed my hand and put it on his thigh and he said, 'You fancy me don't you?'"

After she replied 'no' and pulled her hand away, Brain shouted at her to get out of the car. The woman told the court she was left "distraught" and blamed her own "Catholic frigidity".

But later that night she said she got a call from Brain: "He was speaking in a gentle voice and asked if I could put him to bed."

In his defence Brain insisted there had been "nothing wrong" with members of his congregation giving him massages. He told his second trial "close friends" had given him back rubs to relieve his tension and they had become sexual "very, very" rarely and always consensually.

Brain admitted he would criticise young female members of NOS for their attitudes towards sexuality, but claimed this was "post-modern" attempt to encourage assertiveness.

"This kind of thinking had a profound effect on the development of the third wave of feminism and I regret none of it," he told jurors.

The women who Brain summoned to his bedroom gave a very different account in their evidence during his trials.

"It was what I did to survive at that time," one said. "I didn't have the freedom to consent. I was frightened all the time."

Asked by Brain's defence barrister why they kept returning, the women said they feared being cut out of the movement which had become their life.

One told the court: "He was somebody who was respected by the church, he was supported by the church. He was my priest. Who was I to question his authority?"

Another woman - who told jurors Brain had pushed her down onto a bed and raped her in the early 1980s - described being "brainwashed" and made financially dependent on him.

Witnesses said the homebase team - known by some as the "Lycra lovelies" due to the revealing clothing they wore as they did Brain's housework - were "like slaves" who would sleep on the floor of Brain's office at night.

Throughout his retrial Brain continued to reject his previous convictions, compelling prosecutors to recall victims to court and describe for a second time their experience of how they were sexually assaulted.

Recalled witnesses included a woman who Brain was found to have sexually assaulted in her bed while she was traumatised after helping people locate the bodies of friends and relatives killed in the Hillsborough disaster.

NOS came to an abrupt and dramatic end in 1995 when a former member approached Stephen Lowe, then archdeacon of Sheffield, to warn him the movement had become a cult in which Brain was abusing his congregation.

Lowe, who later became a bishop, had been an enthusiastic supporter of NOS and waved away concerns from fellow clergy as early as 1992.

But the archdeacon told the court he had noticed Brain - who was ordained in the cassock worn by Robert de Niro in the 1986 film The Mission - becoming "something of a messianic" figure.

On hearing the whistleblowers's account that Brain's followers had been "putting him to bed with sexual favours," he told the court he confronted the NOS leader.

In response to claims he had had sexual relationships with up to 40 women in NOS, Brain is said to have told Lowe: "I thought it was more."

The Church of England sent Brain to a psychiatrist, who he told he had been "obsessed with sex since the age of 10," according to a report disclosed as evidence in his trials.

Brain resigned shortly before the broadcast of BBC documentary in 1995 in which he said: "For a priest in a church setting, I would have to say I was involved in improper sexual conduct with a number of women".

Though the scandal devastated the NOS community and made for lurid headlines in the country's newspapers, for some it had not come out of the blue.

During one of the trials, the court heard that, years before allegations against Brain became public, one St Thomas's staff member had been shot down in a meeting for questioning whether it was "appropriate" for "scantily young women" to be seen coming and going from the priest's family home.

Mark Stibbe, the church's curate, told the trial he had also warned Lowe that Brain was growing unaccountable and NOS was heading for "disaster". The archdeacon was said to have replied: "We don't conduct witch hunts in the Sheffield diocese."

As the scandal faded from newspaper front pages, Brain changed his name and disappeared from the public eye. He was running a design consultancy in Wilmslow, Cheshire, when in 2021 former NOS members first contacted South Yorkshire Police.

In the 1995 documentary, then Bishop of Sheffield David Lunn had said: "If people want to set up an investigation, good luck to them. I don't think it would serve any useful purpose. I think we know what happened."

Following Brain's convictions three decades later, the Diocese of Sheffield struck a very different tone, announcing an independent safeguarding review into "institutional failures".

"What happened was an appalling abuse of power and leadership that should never have occurred," said the Right Reverend Dr Pete Wilcox.

title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
content:
Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect.

Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers.

That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172.

The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise.

Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran.

Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies.

Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave.

She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house".

"There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive."

She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control.

"You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said.

Lucy is one of the parents who attend a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast.

Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living.

She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm."

"We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added.

Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher.

He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%.

"It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI.

Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him.

"The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got."

The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university.

"I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country."

'It's getting worse'

Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes.

"Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said.

"I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home.

"Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm."

Naomi said a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices.

She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills.

Terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments, Naomi added.

"I'm really saddened," she said.

"The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care."

Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden.

"It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said.

She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money".

"You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating."

It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today.

This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers.

Head of Energy Policy at the Consumer Council Raymond Gormley said: "This increase has been driven by the continued volatility in wholesale energy costs, caused by geopolitics in the Middle East.

"I suspect some of the other unregulated suppliers may follow suit and increase their tariffs."

Gas prices outside the greater Belfast also rose on Thursday.

Firmus energy has announced an 8.98% rise for 77,000 domestic and small business customers in the Ten Towns network area from 1 October.

That means a typical annual gas bill will rise by around £87.

It comes after an increase of 15.65% in July 2026.

What support is available?

Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month.

It will be applied automatically without the need for an application.

The reduction is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market.

The schemes are being funded by the UK government.

Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter.

The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go.

That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up.

Last month, applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users.

It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government.

Two thirds of homes in Northern Ireland use home heating oil, the cost of which has also soared in recent months due to the US conflict with Iran.

Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year.

title: An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded
content:
All the ingredients of a typical Northern Ireland crisis have been in place for the past week except for one – violence.

A stand-off - over a proposed Orange Order parade in Portadown, opposed by nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.

Verbal clashes between politicians, late-night negotiations, appeals for calm and a major security operation have all been in the mix.

However, the Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown has not descended into disorder or trouble on the streets.

Sometimes in Northern Ireland, the definition of success is "nobody got hurt".

The crisis is not over, and fears of an outbreak of street violence remain, but everything is under control at the moment.

The truth is few predicted a relatively peaceful week when the crisis first erupted.

It was an extraordinary seven days.

Tension started to build after the Parades Commission, which regulates marches, gave the go-ahead for the controversial Orange Order parade in Portadown to pass along the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.

That was on a Friday afternoon.

Within 24 hours the issue was being battled out at the High Court in Belfast during an urgent Saturday hearing which ended up lasting more than 13 hours..

Sitting under the same roof were those involved in the dispute – Portadown Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition – headed by Nigel Dawson and Breandán Mac Cionnaith respectively.

They sat within a matter of feet from each other but their positions were worlds apart.

Court proceedings ended in the early hours of Sunday morning, with the parade given the go-ahead.

All involved then made the 30-mile journey through the night from Belfast to Portadown ahead of the scheduled start to the Orange parade at 08:00 BST.

By that stage, their route along the Garvaghy Road had been blocked.

Up to 1,000 people were standing in the middle of the road, many of them linking arms.

Some of them were prominent members of Sinn Féin, which helped turn the parade controversy into a political crisis at Stormont.

A mile away, outside Drumcree Church, the 35 Orangemen who were hoping to march went back inside.

Torrential rain meant everyone got cold and wet, particularly the protesters but the road remained blocked and the parade was thwarted.

Police told the Orangemen not even to try to walk down the road.

And so the stand-off began.

Since then there has been frenetic activity behind-the-scenes, mainly at Hillsborough Castle, to try to break the deadlock.

Four days of talks took place but by Thursday night it was clear they were going nowhere.

At Stormont, the power-sharing executive came close to collapse. In the end, it wobbled but it did not fall down.

Unionists accused some members of Sinn Féin of being lawmakers who became lawbreakers. They insisted they were simply supporting a community that needed their help.

Expect that argument to continue in the days and weeks ahead.

In the meantime, the focus now switches back to Belfast High Court, for an appeal hearing on Monday.

The residents' coalition is trying to overturn the decision to give the march the go-ahead.

Although the court is important, nobody is taking their eye off the situation on the ground in Portadown, especially the police.

The Orangemen still want to walk. The protesters are standing by, just in case.

The Drumcree stand-off remains tense.

The hope is that the only battles which take place in the coming days are in the Belfast courtroom and the Stormont chamber, and not on the streets of Portadown.

What's the background to the Garvaghy Road dispute?

The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident.

However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, mainly Catholic or nationalist areas.

The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree parade route but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against it.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years, until recent events.

Read more about the history of the parade.

title: Capital gains tax rise would deter equity investors, wealth bosses warn
content:
Emma Dunkley in London

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

Chief executives of the UK’s largest investment sites have warned against increasing capital gains tax in the upcoming Budget. They say it could deter savers from investing in the stock market, creating a conflict with one of the government’s stated aims.

CGT is charged on profits from selling assets such as shares, businesses and second homes. The main higher rate was increased in the 2024 Budget from 20 per cent to 24 per cent. The annual allowance — the amount exempt from CGT — was also cut in half to £3,000.

Concerns that CGT could rise further have intensified in recent weeks, as it sits outside the Labour government’s commitment not to increase taxes on working people.

But wealth management bosses urged the Treasury against making the tax more punitive, noting that it could undermine the government’s attempts to encourage more people to invest and back the UK’s equity market.

Matt Benchener, chief executive of Hargreaves Lansdown, told the FT: “The government wants to get more Britons investing, but raising capital gains tax would work directly against that goal.

“By some estimates, more than £600bn sits in excess cash , its value being eroded by inflation. Taxing investment returns more heavily would be another deterrent for cautious savers who need to be encouraged to take the next step and invest.”

“They say they are trying to foster a retail investing culture, but their policies are doing the opposite,” said Michael Summersgill, chief executive of AJ Bell. “The chancellor should be looking to encourage long-term investing by simplifying tax rules instead of continually layering on complexity and cost.”

Richard Wilson, chief executive at Interactive Investor, said: “You cannot build a nation of investors while increasing the tax on investing. Higher capital gains tax reduces the incentive to take risk, back businesses and build long-term wealth.

“At a time when the government says it wants growth, raising CGT would send entirely the wrong signal to millions of savers and investors whose capital helps power the economy.”

Investment sites tend to charge dealing fees when investors make trades — such as selling their shares.

Other wealth managers point out that increasing CGT will not necessarily generate more revenue for the government.

Steven Levin, chief executive of Quilter, noted that investors could end up deferring the sale of assets as a result. “Any changes to CGT therefore need to be assessed not only through a fiscal lens, but also through their impact on investment activity, entrepreneurship and the UK’s attractiveness as a destination for capital.”

Higher CGT could also lead more people to invest in gilts, which do not incur CGT, instead of shares. Peter Hargreaves, co-founder of Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “If there is less advantage in investing for growth, [people] will change, they will look at low-coupon gilts, which are CGT free.”

title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she had given birth to his babies, judge rules
content:
A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit".

The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John in the judgement, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined £500.

The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around £30,000 over the course of two years.

But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her.

The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on.

In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man.

He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday.

Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos.

At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background.

Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024.

However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile.

The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born.

The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children.

She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said.

In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way".

She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend.

"Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said.

The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part.

title: The right and wrong lessons to learn from Spain’s housing crisis
content:
John Burn-Murdoch

Published October 3 2026

Although housing crises have been smouldering across much of the high-income world for a decade or more, they have generally tended to rank some way down the political agenda.

That may be about to change, with reports suggesting Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez is considering calling an early election in a bid to resolve mounting public and political discontent over spiralling rents and prices after his flagship housing bill was rejected by parliament on Friday.

Mass protests were sparked recently by the case of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. She was served an eviction notice after her previously rent-controlled flat was bought by a corporate landlord which sought to increase the rent to a level well above her monthly pension income.

Much of the anger has centred on the role of so-called “vulture funds” in the rental market — Sanchez’s party has proposed banning large-scale investors from buying homes until 2028. But if policymakers and tenants alike want to see durable improvements and to avoid unintended negative consequences, it’s worth taking a step back and looking at what is, in truth, a much deeper problem, both in Spain and in other countries.

Consider the many recent cases in the UK and Ireland where protesters have similarly rallied in opposition to evictions — often not by greedy corporate landlords but by local councils seeking to move rent-controlled properties on to new low-income tenants. These happen after the former tenant passes away or moves out but their family members refuse to leave.

The specifics of such cases are very different but they all speak to the same problem: acute housing shortages. A landlord — whether the corporate or “mom-and-pop” variety — increases rents only when they are confident they will find someone willing to pay the higher price. The bidding wars resulting from shortages provide fertile ground. Spain has built fewer homes per capita than virtually any other high-income country over the past 10 years . More than 50 per cent of its young adults now live with their parents, up from 33 per cent in 2005, and rents have risen more steeply than almost anywhere else.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The reason the children of British and Irish social housing tenants are desperate to keep hold of the homes after tenancies expire — and why waiting lists for those cost-controlled homes are so long — is the acute shortage of properties in these countries. The UK and Ireland each lack roughly one in seven homes they need to adequately house today’s populations.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Spain’s problems are on both the supply and demand sides. Its housebuilding crunch has coincided with a population boom fuelled in large part by a conscious effort by Sánchez to boost immigration . On top of that, surging inflows of tourists and digital nomads mean the market-clearing rent is often set not by local incomes but by those of affluent visitors. Courting workers and high-spending visitors from overseas is sound economic policy, but it requires a joined-up approach on the supply side in the form of much greater housebuilding — some of which could be funded through increased tourist taxes.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The government’s proposals so far amount to a patchwork of sticking plasters that address some of the symptoms but not the underlying cause. Stronger protections for existing tenants and bans on investment will not ease shortage-driven pressure on rents and prices. Nor will they house the millions of young adults whose lives and careers are on hold while they are forced to share a roof with their parents.

In this regard Spain may want to look to Ireland, where policymakers last year watered down rent controls over concerns they were contributing to weak rates of new construction in the rental sector, exacerbating the underlying causes of the disease whose symptoms they were intended to treat.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Fixing housing crises is far easier said than done. If mounting costs and worsening shortages were simple to reverse sustainably, they would not be afflicting so many different places with a wide variety of policy and economic environments.

But to stand any chance of lasting success, policymakers must ensure they go beyond shallow and often counter-productive regulations or selective protections for those lucky enough to already be renting, and wrestle instead with the more challenging reforms that could put downward pressure on rents and prices for all and for good.
