title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
content:
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.

Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.

Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".

Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.

Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.

Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.

So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?

Spain accused of self-interest

Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.

Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.

That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.

"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.

"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."

Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.

"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."

Rising Chinese investment

According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.

"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.

But there's also the question of security.

On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.

This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.

MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.

"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.

Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".

Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.

"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.

"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."

More emerging alliances

Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.

Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.

In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.

Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.

No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.

"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.

In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".

Greece's shift

Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.

In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.

In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.

There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".

He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.

With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.

But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.

He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.

That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.

Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.

However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.

Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

title: 东京通胀加速 大幅高于日本央行目标
content:
随着部分临时性政府政策效应消退，东京核心通胀指标大幅走高，印证日本央行在加快政策正常化步伐后，将继续上调基准利率的立场。
日本总务省周五公布的数据显示，东京9月剔除生鲜食品的消费者物价指数同比上涨2.7%。该数据高于经济学家预期中值2.3%，上月增幅为1.8%。
此前，东京扩大育儿补贴以及夏季水费减免政策压低了该项通胀指标，因此市场普遍预期本次数据将出现加速上涨。CPI的飙升印证了日本央行的担忧：通胀上行风险或将推动核心物价趋势突破2%的目标。

title: 软银投资者暂放信用风险 评估人工智能上行潜力
content:
软银 集团的股票投资者暂时搁置对这家日本企业融资成本走高的担忧，聚焦其人工智能押注带来的潜在回报。
OpenAI新模型GPT-6 Astra重燃市场信心，投资者看好孙正义向ChatGPT开发商承诺投入的650亿美元，软银股价9月实现四个月以来首次月度上涨。得益于OpenAI最新一轮300亿美元融资计划（估值1.4万亿美元），该股四周内上涨24%。芯片子公司Arm股价回升，也提振市场信心，投资者相信这家科技投资集团有能力偿还不断增加的债务。
与此同时，由于市场持续担忧AI安全、成本飙升与行业竞争，软银信用违约互换（CDS）价格飙升至2023年以来最高水平。软银CDS与股票走势出现分化，这与 甲骨文 公司股价下跌形成对比；甲骨文援引不可抗力条款，规避激增的数据中心成本。
圣坦德·伯恩斯坦香港董事总经理戴大为在谈及软银时表示：“从股票投资角度，我们对其融资的技术细节不会过度关注。只要公司能够完成融资，股票层面的故事就十分亮眼。软银持有Arm股权，而Arm是智能体AI与服务器CPU需求增长的最大受益者。”
Arm与其他芯片厂商预测，到2030年，中央处理器的市场需求规模可达数千亿美元。元平台Muse等服务用户越来越多地让AI智能体编写代码、操作网页浏览器，通用计算订单持续增加。戴大为预估该市场规模最高可达3300亿美元，他称Arm的订单前景同样向好。
Arm股价从6月高点近乎腰斩后，现已企稳回升，上月涨幅约20%。软银持有这家芯片设计公司近90%股份，Arm股价回暖巩固了软银的财务状况，缓解部分从信贷市场传导而来的恐慌情绪。Arm是软银资产价值的核心组成部分。
除Arm外，孙正义在AI赛道广泛布局，覆盖机器人、数据中心、能源领域，令部分股票投资者感到安心。尽管这位亿万富豪对OpenAI的巨额押注仍存隐忧，但软银计划拓展其他AI赛道（如建设数据中心、收购ABB机器人业务），投资者认为，无论平台竞争最终花落谁家，这些资产都具备上行空间。
软银投资版图广泛，旗下拥有拥有数百万用户的电信运营商软银公司。这家无线运营商正借力日本国内对AI的旺盛需求，建设数据中心，并提供一整套企业服务。
彭博行业研究分析师柯克·布德里称：“如果OpenAI发展不及预期，市场情绪会大幅恶化，但软银仍持有其他领域资产。在日本市场，能这样全面受益全球AI热潮的标的十分罕见。”
软银股价相对实时净资产价值的折价进一步扩大，为看好AI增长的投资者提供入场机会。彭博行业研究数据显示，截至9月29日，软银股价较净资产价值折价24%，高于年初至今20%的均值。
资管一号基金经理西田拓实表示：“一旦出现合适的催化因素，股价估值重估的潜力确实存在。曾经市场还讨论过软银股价相对净资产溢价交易。”
但西田拓实称，由于AI开发企业竞争激烈、融资成本持续走高，他更倾向直接投资AI硬件供应商，例如存储芯片厂商铠侠。对比东证指数基准权重，他持有的软银仓位更低。
持类似观点的投资者不在少数。AI模型赛道竞争加剧、债务规模攀升的担忧，持续压制软银股价。
软银上月完成规模111亿美元债券发行，创下史上最大规模企业垃圾债发行纪录，为孙正义宏大的AI投资计划筹措资金。尽管认购需求充足，压低了发行定价，但融资成本整体仍高于过往水平。
S3 Partners数据显示，部分投资者押注软银股价下跌，本周流通股的空头占比升至2.36%，创年内新高。
斯帕克斯资产管理分析师韩志浩表示，软银股价长期相对净资产折价，说明股票市场已经计入一定程度的信用风险。“若CDS利差继续走阔，净资产价值进一步增长对股价的拉动作用将会受限。”
即便如此，软银股价自6月高点回落之后已有所修复，今年累计上涨约52%。彭博汇总数据显示，多数分析师看好后续走势：17个买入评级、6个持有评级、1个卖出评级。分析师给出12个月目标价均值为9061日元（折合57.21美元），对比该股东京市场周四收盘价6701日元。
在6月季度，软银依靠 英特尔 股权录得净利润，让这家科技投资集团有充足底气，等待OpenAI及其他数十亿美元AI项目兑现收益。
里索纳控股策略师武井博树称：“倘若AI热潮最终演变为泡沫并破裂，在高杠杆投资的加持下，软银将遭受重创。但从最新财报来看，高融资成本更多被视作尾部风险，市场普遍认为本次发债是为成长性投资筹措资金。”

title: 美国新墨西哥州寻求对Meta罚款400亿美元
content:
美国新墨西哥州周四请求法官下令Meta Platforms支付350亿至400亿美元的罚款；此前，在一桩源于剑桥分析公司（Cambridge Analytica）丑闻的诉讼中，陪审团认定该公司在Facebook用户数据隐私问题上误导了该州消费者。
新墨西哥州的律师在一次诉讼听证会上提出了这一请求；该诉讼源于一项曝光：一家曾服务于唐纳德·特朗普2016年总统竞选活动的英国政治咨询公司（剑桥分析公司），通过一款第三方应用程序，在未经用户同意的情况下获取了多达8700万Facebook用户的个人数据。
陪审团于9月25日作出了裁决。主持此次庭审的法官弗朗西斯·马修（Francis Mathew）将决定Meta需支付的罚款金额。
在听证会上，Meta与新墨西哥州的律师就罚款的适当数额发生了分歧；Meta主张，该州寻求的罚款金额与其在庭审中重点指控的违规行为并不相符。
这起诉讼于2021年提起，指控Meta向新墨西哥州Facebook用户撒谎，隐瞒了关于谁能获取用户数据、公司如何处理平台上发布的仇恨言论与虚假信息，以及其他内部政策的实情。该州指称，Meta明知第三方拥有广泛获取用户个人数据的权限，却在仇恨言论或其他有害内容有利于公司经济利益时，对这些内容予以容忍。
陪审团审查了该公司及其高管就相关问题发表的29项声明，认定其中26项具有误导性。陪审团指出，根据接触到每一项误导性声明的Facebook用户或新墨西哥州居民人数计算，该公司违反新墨西哥州消费者保护法的次数超过了4300万次。
Meta公司的律师在庭审中辩称，这些声明只是被断章取义的片段；公司也曾多次承认，其在处理虚假信息或隐私问题方面做得并不完美。
根据新墨西哥州法律，法官有权决定针对每次违规行为对Meta处以多少罚款，最高可达5000美元。
在周四举行的听证会上，代表新墨西哥州的律师兰迪·麦金（Randi McGinn）表示，若针对每一项违规行为都处以5000美元的最高罚款，根据美国宪法关于正当程序的保护条款，由此产生的总罚款额将过高。
不过，麦金指出，法官仍应判令该公司支付一笔数额可观的罚款，以确保对其产生实质性影响。
麦金表示，法院应当用 Meta 唯一能听懂的语言——即金钱和股价——来与该公司对话。她指出，350亿至400亿美元的罚款金额（约占根据州法律可能判处的罚款总额的20%）既能对股价产生影响，又符合宪法赋予 Meta 的正当程序权利。
在周四举行的听证会上，Meta的律师马特·尼科尔森（Matt Nicholson）称该州提出的罚款要求是“一笔天文数字般的罚款，显然违反了多项宪法条款”。
Meta 在法庭文件中敦促法官马修将罚款上限设定为34.5亿美元。该公司在文件中辩称，尽管陪审团认定 Meta 的陈述具有误导性，但证据显示 Meta 并未出售用户数据，且新墨西哥州也未能证明有任何消费者真正受到了误导。
法官表示，预计将于本月晚些时候作出裁决。

title: 特朗普赴深红州得克萨斯州造势 呼吁选民支持帕克斯顿
content:
美国总统特朗普前往深红州得克萨斯州，为共和党参议院候选人肯·帕克斯顿动员选民热情，正式开启11月中期选举前为期一个月的密集竞选造势。
“我们非常需要肯，这也是我来到这里的原因。”特朗普周四在得州达拉斯郊区登顿市的彼得比尔特汽车公司厂区举办的活动上表示。
特朗普的得州之行是周四两州造势行程的第一站，随后他将赴边境另一侧的俄克拉荷马州参加集会。这两个州在他三次总统竞选中都轻松拿下，此番到访凸显共和党当前处境凶险，其国会控制权岌岌可危。
特朗普周五还将到访阿拉巴马州，周六前往俄亥俄州，为本党争取选举优势。但此举能否争取到足够选情尚存疑问。距离选举日已不足五周，多项民调显示，共和党在关键的众议院选区落后于民主党。爱荷华、佐治亚、俄亥俄等州的选战竞争加剧，共和党保住参议院控制权的希望也愈发渺茫。
特朗普支持率跌至历史低点，高昂生活成本以及对伊战争推高油价，引发选民不满。
得州总检察长帕克斯顿的参选历程，折射出共和党在部分传统票仓州遭遇的困境。帕克斯顿在激烈的初选中击败了参议员约翰·科宁，但如今在民调中落后于州众议员詹姆斯·塔拉里科。塔拉里科有望成为自1988年以来首位当选联邦参议员的得州民主党人。
特朗普在演讲中多次呼吁选民支持帕克斯顿，而他此前曾批评过这位候选人。在上个月的共和党大会上，总统多次吐槽帕克斯顿的着装与演讲风格。周四特朗普再度调侃帕克斯顿，称他有时“很讨人嫌”，但欣赏其个人忠诚度。
“这场选举至关重要，我想说，他是我的多年好友。”特朗普说道。
特朗普的背书，是帕克斯顿在激烈初选中击败科宁的关键。部分党内高层，包括前州众议院议长乔·斯特劳斯与战略家卡尔·罗夫，都质疑帕克斯顿能否担当共和党在得州的领军人物。
上个月特朗普还在达拉斯举办中期选举大会，试图提振共和党士气，但这场活动未能扭转本党选情。这也表明，对于许多陷入胶着选战的候选人而言，总统低迷的民调数据更多是拖累而非助力。
上周有消息称，帕克斯顿向捐赠者与游说者坦言，这场大会在政治层面损害了他的竞选。当被问及帕克斯顿的这番言论时，特朗普回避了该问题，坚称大会取得了很高的电视收视率。
随着全美选民对特朗普好感度下滑，他在得州的支持率同样受挫。2024年他曾在该州以近14个百分点的优势获胜。近期民调显示，他在得州净支持率为负。得州选民当下最关心高物价与对伊战争，并且在这两件事上对总统评价很低。

title: 韩国9月通胀率回落至2.9%，燃油价格仍高企
content:
周五公布的数据显示，韩国9月份消费者价格指数（CPI）同比上涨2.9%；能源成本依然高企，而农产品价格则有所下降。
根据韩国数据和统计部发布的数据，9月份CPI涨幅回落至2%区间，较8月份3.1%的涨幅有所放缓。
9月份，柴油价格大幅上涨20%，汽油价格也急剧攀升了11.8%。
韩国高度依赖进口来满足其能源需求。

title: 美联储洛根：仍需进一步加息 目标至少为加50个基点
content:
达拉斯联邦储备银行行长洛里·洛根表示，美联储必须继续加息，以彻底抑制通胀，同时她提出美债收益率上行也有助于放缓经济。
“我目前预估，利率目标区间还需上调50个基点或更多，才能妥善平衡我们双重使命目标对应的前景与风险。”洛根周四在达拉斯联储一场活动的准备发言稿中表示。
洛根在就任达拉斯联储行长前，曾在纽约联储市场部门任职二十余年。她还提到过去数周美国国债收益率持续走高。她称市场参与者向她表示，本轮收益率上涨最初源于市场预期经济强劲增长、美联储中性利率抬升，但模型当前显示期限溢价（投资者持有长期债券相比短期债券所要求的额外回报）也在上升。
“更高的期限溢价能够放缓经济，从而减少货币政策收紧的需要。”洛根说道，她是今年美联储利率决策机构联邦公开市场委员会的投票委员。
由于通胀降温进程陷入停滞，政策制定者在9月会议上加息25个基点，为三年来首次加息。该次会议上官员的预期中值显示，今年至少还会再加息一次。债券今年遭遇抛售，30年期美债收益率自6月以来上行64个基点，即0.64个百分点。
洛根的部分同僚本周表示，美联储可以耐心等待，择机实施下一次加息。美联储副主席菲利普·杰斐逊与纽约联储行长约翰· 威廉姆斯 （二人与主席凯文·沃什有时被称作美联储三巨头）称，美联储可以等待，观察未来几周的数据变化，再作出政策决定。
上述言论压低了市场对于美联储在10月27-28日会议加息的预期。根据联邦基金利率期货定价，当前投资者认为下月加息概率仅为28%，本周早些时候该概率为70%。本月之后，美联储官员下一次会议在12月。
洛根曾在2023年的演讲中详细介绍她参考的各类美债市场模型。她表示会持续观察收益率走势以及经济其他方面，以此判断何种利率水平能够对经济形成一定抑制效果。
洛根说：“至少，对目标区间再进行数次上调，才能抵消联邦公开市场委员会去年秋季出于风险考量作出的降息操作。”她此处指美联储去年累计75个基点的加息。“但最终目标应当是让货币政策保持适度紧缩，使经济走向同时维持充分就业与物价稳定的轨道。”

title: 耐克计划进一步裁员，预计本财年营收将大幅下滑
content:
耐克 周四预计全年营收将出现大幅下滑，并宣布新一轮裁员计划并重组全球业务部门。在首席执行官埃利奥特・希尔领导下，该公司正深化重组以应对日益严峻的中国市场困境。
周四这份疲软的业绩预期凸显出，耐克面临的挑战很可能至少还要持续几个季度，尤其是在中国市场，该地区第一季度的销售额按固定汇率计算暴跌了26%——这加剧了投资者对希尔扭转局势进展速度的担忧。受此影响，耐克股价在周四盘后交易中下跌了8.5%。
在希尔（Hill）上任的头两年里，该公司一直致力于重振增长，具体举措包括重新聚焦跑步等核心运动项目，以及重建与批发零售商的合作关系。然而分析师指出，公司面临的困境在很大程度上源于未能推出足够多且极具吸引力的新品，从而导致促销和打折活动增多。
该公司第一财季的营收也未达分析师预期，同时宣布了运营模式的调整，包括裁员以及将原有的四个地理大区重组为三个：美洲区、亚太及大中华区，以及 EMEA（欧洲、中东和非洲）区。此外，该公司计划在印度建立一个新园区，以利用当地强大的业务能力和人才资源。
耐克表示，公司尚未确定此次重组将涉及的裁员人数，并将于2027年开始通知相关员工。
该计划建立在以往多轮裁员（包括今年早些时候宣布的一轮）的基础上，预计到2031财年将节省约25亿美元的成本，其中大部分节约将在2029财年和2030财年实现。
耐克预计2027财年的营收将出现高个位数的下滑。根据LSEG汇编的数据，分析师平均预计其全年营收将下降约2%。
中国市场销售额再次大幅下滑
中国市场历来是耐克（Nike）的利润增长引擎，但近几个季度表现尤为疲软，这主要是因为国际竞争对手和本土运动服饰企业正不断扩大市场份额。投资者密切关注任何好转迹象，而分析师指出，这在很大程度上将取决于本土产品的创新表现。
耐克在中国的销售额已连续九个季度下滑，且在最新报告期内跌幅进一步扩大。该地区贡献了耐克约15%的年收入，是继北美以及欧洲、中东和非洲（EMEA）之后的第三大市场。

title: 沙特空袭也门首都萨那！胡塞武装遭受重大伤亡！大举增兵，美“西奥多·罗斯福”号航母已出动！国际油价狂飙
content:
来源：期货日报
早上好，一起来看下重要资讯！
布伦特 原油 价格突破100美元/桶
截至10月1日收盘，布伦特原油价格上涨5.19%，报103.11美元/桶。
消息面上，中东局势再度紧张。
也门西南省份战事加剧 30名胡塞武装人员被打死
据央视新闻援引也门共和国电视台1日报道称， 也门西南部塔伊兹省多个战线战事加剧。
该报道援引政府军声明说， 政府军当天在塔伊兹省南部地区与胡塞武装激战，打死30名胡塞武装人员，打伤50人 。
另据也门政府军消息， 自1日清晨以来，塔伊兹省5条战线持续交战，政府军和胡塞武装均遭受重大人员伤亡 。
一名不愿透露姓名的军方人士称，当天战事从清晨开始，双方进行猛烈炮击，并发动无人机攻击。截至1日下午战斗仍在持续。政府军加大地面军事行动力度。此外，沙特阿拉伯战机当天也对塔伊兹省受胡塞武装控制的多处阵地发动空袭。
胡塞武装军事发言人叶海亚·萨雷亚1日在社交媒体发布声明称， 过去24小时内，沙特战机对也门塔伊兹、萨达和焦夫省发动47次空袭和导弹袭击，袭击目标包括通信网络等。
此外，也门胡塞武装方面证实，当地时间10月1日夜间，沙特对也门萨那、萨达省、塔伊兹省、阿姆朗省等胡塞武装控制区进行了空袭。 这是9月3日局势升级以来，沙特首次空袭胡塞武装控制下的也门首都萨那。
近期，胡塞武装加大对政府军攻势，并宣布对支持也门政府的沙特实施海上禁运。胡塞武装已攻占港口城市穆哈、丕林岛等战略要地。也门政府方面9月11日说，胡塞武装已控制该国整个西部海岸，并将攻势推进至南部拉赫季省。
美媒：美军向中东增派第三艘航母及最多1万名士兵
据援引美国官员的话报道， 五角大楼正向中东派遣第三个航母战斗群及更多海军陆战队两栖舰艇，预计新增9000至10000名美军，相关舰艇、战机和人员将在11月底前抵达。
报道称， 目前“乔治·H·W·布什”号和“乔治·华盛顿”号航母已部署中东，“西奥多·罗斯福”号航母日前从圣迭戈启程，“马金岛”号两栖戒备群也已出发。 若“乔治·华盛顿”号届时仍留在当地，美军将在中东同时部署三个航母战斗群，为4月以来首次。此外，美军近期还延长了防空部队及陆军第82空降师等部队的部署。
报道还称，目前中东已有超过5万名美军和约20艘美国海军舰艇。 此次增兵之际，美国总统特朗普正考虑若美伊未能达成协议，在中期选举后恢复对伊朗的军事打击。第三艘航母若继续留在当地，将为美方提供更多军事选项和火力。
霍尔木兹海峡仍“不太平”
据央视新闻报道，当地时间10月1日，伊朗“波斯湾海峡管理局”发表声明称，近期霍尔木兹海峡发生多起油轮遇袭事件，其中最近遇袭的三艘油轮均为阿联酋拥有或租赁。 调查显示，“Al Ruwais”号、“Sinbad”号和“Mersin Prosperity”号油轮在过去两个月中曾多次通过霍尔木兹海峡，上述三艘油轮的名称曾出现在“波斯湾海峡管理局”最新更新的违规名单中。
另据央视新闻报道，当地时间10月1日，英国海上贸易行动办公室发布通报称，其收到第三方报告，一艘油轮在通过霍尔木兹海峡时遭不明飞行物击中并引发火灾。
四季度 集运指数 （欧线）期货如何走？
国庆假期前，集运市场交投趋于谨慎，集运指数（欧线）期货主力合约从高位回落。
与此同时，现货市场同样偏弱运行。上海航运交易所发布的数据显示，9月30日上海出口集装箱综合运价指数为3662.30点，较上期下跌0.7%；其中，上海港出口至欧洲基本港的市场运价为2199美元/TEU，较上期下跌4.9%，地中海航线基本港的市场运价为2996美元/TEU，较上期下跌2.3%。
“节前集运市场交投趋于谨慎，盘面缺乏方向性指引。”海通期货航运研究负责人雷悦表示，随着2610合约进入交割月，资金加速离场，2611和2612合约尚未出现明显的增仓迹象，市场等待更多现货端的指引。
船司报价有所下调。雷悦表示，OOCL将10月6日至14日的现货报价下调至3000~3100美元/TEU，目前第41周现货报价均值约3000美元/TEU，后续需关注马士基第43周开舱价格以及其他船司的跟进情况。
值得注意的是，此前台风造成上海、香港等港口拥堵的现象已基本消退。据雷悦介绍，上海港拥堵指数持续回落，9月27日降至53.5万，正式跌破56.6万的基线水平，在港船数也由188艘降至119艘。随着港口运行逐步恢复正常，前期拥堵对有效运力的“缓冲”作用正在减弱。
展望四季度，东证衍生品研究院航运研究员兰淅表示，集运市场需求仍具备一定韧性，欧洲制造业和投资需求仍将支撑欧线货运量。当前，消费补库尚未明显启动，但欧美库存已经历较长时间的去化，随着年底旺季来临以及潜在的补库需求释放，四季度后段集运市场需求仍存。
供给端压力或逐步增加。兰淅表示，10月下旬集运市场计划运力明显回升，若节后港口拥堵的情况进一步改善，供应压力将有所缓解。不过，前期港口拥堵已吞噬部分红海通行情况下船舶周转效率改善的预期，潜在有效运力释放仍会受到一定的约束。
谈及后市，雷悦表示，10月上旬运价波动及10月下旬船司宣涨等情况值得关注。从历史来看，船司涨价与SCFIS指数上涨存在一定时滞，涨价能否兑现仍需观察。11—12月，还需关注空班及苏伊士运河复航等因素，若11月出现较多空班，将对运价形成支撑。不过，随着12月苏伊士运河复航，新增运力供给可能限制运价上涨空间。

title: 韩国9月通胀保持高位 料支持韩国央行维持紧缩倾向
content:
韩国9月通胀保持高位，显示物价压力持续，料支持韩国央行维持货币政策紧缩倾向。
韩国政府周五公布的数据显示，9月消费者价格同比上涨2.9%，低于8月的3.1%，与经济学家的预估中值一致。
剔除波动较大的食品和能源价格后，核心通胀率为2.8%，低于8月的3.4%，也与预期一致。这表明，除了能源成本高企的影响之外，核心通胀压力仍然较高。
韩国央行7月和8月连续加息，基准利率上调至3%。最新通胀数据可能进一步强化其紧缩倾向。决策者此前警告称，经济增长强劲、通胀居高不下以及房价上涨，可能需要进一步提高利率。
韩国央行8月公布的未来六个月利率预测中值为3.25%，意味着可能还会加息一次。不过，韩国央行行长申铉松表示，这一预测显示未来收紧政策的步伐将较为渐进。

title: 麦当劳荃湾铺位以1.2亿港元卖出 39年内升值14倍
content:
据报道， 麦当劳 以1.2亿港元（约1530万美元）的价格出售了位于香港荃湾的一家门市。
报道指出，这处面积12251平方英尺的物业在39年内升值14倍，每平方英尺的价格接近10，000港元。
这家门市于1978年开业，是麦当劳在香港新界的首家分店，麦当劳于1987年以800万港元购入该铺位。

title: 特朗普给自己第二任期表现打分：所有方面都是“A+”
content:
美国总统唐纳德・特朗普给自己的第二任期的表现打出了“A+”的高分，尽管民调显示他的支持率已接近历史低位，而且由于民众不满其经济治理表现，共和党似乎很可能在中期选举中丢掉众议院控制权，参议院席位也难保。
特朗普周四在从白宫动身前往德克萨斯州前表示：“在政府工作、经济层面，所有方面，我都给我们打A+。” 他此行将到访彼得比尔特汽车公司（Peterbilt Motors），为自己政府的政绩造势宣传。
本周，特朗普已有两次将宣传失利归咎于自己团队 —— 没能把他就任近两年来取得的各项利好成果宣传到位。周四他又补充称：“媒体对我们并不公平。”
然而，目前美国通胀居高不下，汽油价格突破每加仑 4.40 美元，抵押贷款利率超过 7%。即便是在深红州（共和党传统票仓）的共和党人，也正遭遇严峻阻力，有可能在选举中落败下台。
周四公布的一项民调显示，仅有26%的美国人认可特朗普对经济的处理方式，认可其在应对生活成本问题上表现的人则仅占17%；另有65%的受访者认为，特朗普的政策推高了物价。
特朗普周四还重申了他的预测：自2月下旬美以联合对伊朗发动袭击以来一路飙升的能源价格，很快就会大幅回落。“油价很快就会降下来，”他说，“一旦伊朗那边结束了——而他们眼下已基本处于穷途末路——油价就会下跌。”

title: 印尼央行行长：外汇捍卫力度不变，策略已调整
content:
印尼央行新任行长表示，尽管减少成本高昂的即期市场干预、更多使用衍生品，但捍卫印尼盾的力度保持不变。
“我们在工具上多元化，但维持印尼盾稳定的政策力度不变。”德斯崔·达玛扬蒂行长于周四接受采访时称。这是她上月就任以来的首次专访。
德斯崔本周早些时候披露，目前即期交易仅占全部外汇干预规模的约30%，其余干预操作在离岸与在岸无本金交割远期（NDF）市场开展，以此保护外汇储备。
印尼8月外汇储备规模为1465亿美元。近几个月，随着央行扩大使用无本金交割远期工具，外汇储备规模趋于企稳。
德斯崔称，干预工具组合取决于市场环境，印尼央行会逐案评估美元需求的来源与紧迫程度。央行同时鼓励有债务兑付计划的企业，在并非即刻需要美元时使用衍生品对冲。
但她表示：“如果即期市场美元供给真正萎缩、需求高企，我们别无选择，只能入场干预即期市场。”
“说到底，货币操作是一门艺术。”她补充道。
德斯崔上任以来，印尼盾再度承压。9月初汇率约为1美元兑17700印尼盾，当月晚些时候一度跌破18000。油价上涨、美债收益率走高，冲击包含印尼资产在内的新兴市场资产。印尼盾今年已贬值约7%，是亚洲表现最差的货币。
德斯崔称，印尼央行也在审慎使用离岸无本金交割远期市场，尤其是自去年4月特朗普关税引发全球市场多轮波动之后。此举旨在防止印尼本地交易时段以外，无本金交割远期市场由市场情绪驱动的剧烈波动，在印尼市场开盘后传导至在岸汇率。
面对美元走强、美债收益率上行以及油价高企的冲击，印尼央行的定向调控思路同样体现在货币政策层面。一旦印尼国债与美债之间的利差收窄，资本就会从印尼资产外流，印尼盾随之走弱。
“以相对可控的成本维持投资者获得的利差至关重要。资本没有忠诚度。”她说道，并补充印尼正与菲律宾、印度等新兴经济体竞争国际资本。
印尼央行部分依靠对冲激励等定向举措维持利差，而非单纯依靠加息。德斯崔称，这类举措可为投资者带来约40至50个基点的有效净利差提升，并且已经吸引资金流入国债与印尼央行印尼盾证券（SRBI）。
德斯崔表示，货币政策以稳定为首要目标。她重申，央行在二季度累计加息100个基点，是防范印尼盾风险的前置性举措。被问及后续政策动向时，她强调央行将继续依据数据决策。
她还表示，央行同时希望支持经济增长，因为当前经济尚未达到满负荷产能。通胀目前主要由供给端因素驱动，仅依靠利率工具抑制物价压力的效果有限。
谈及央行新增的、要助力经济增长的广义政策目标时，德斯崔称这不代表将增长置于稳定之上。实体经济增长、创造就业的前提是稳定。“我们各方协同发力，持续推动经济增长，追求可持续的增长。”

title: 花旗：欧元短期存在跌至1.0850美元的风险
content:
花旗分析师警告称，虽然他们没有改变对欧元的预测，但欧元跌破公允价值的风险上升，可能最低跌至1.0850美元。
“作为背景，我们对欧元/美元0-3个月的预测为1.1350，这主要基于中期经济增长和利差，”分析师Daniel Tobon、Brian Levine和Osamu Takashima写道。“现在汇率明显跌破这一水平，我们认为存在下行风险，短期内可能进一步跌至1.0850”。
他们指出：“但这并非预测调整，而是反映出如果相对利率保持不变，而外围欧债利差扩大、欧洲银行业持续抛售，欧元兑美元可能在多大程度上跌破公允价值”。
他们表示：“我们认为周五公布的非农就业数据不太可能成为重要影响因素”。

title: 'It could cost me £10k but I need the money now': Why Gen Z are opting out of pensions
content:
Until early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.

But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".

He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.

But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now.

"People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."

Future problems

All employees will be automatically enrolled, external in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.

A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top.

But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.

That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension, it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.

Hassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.

But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.

Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can.

According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not.

However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".

'How can I save for a house?'

Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.

A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent.

Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now.

"How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."

'Think of your future self'

April Leeson, from The Private Office, a chartered financial advice firm, says she would always advise people to not stop paying into their pensions if they can help it, even if that means reducing their contributions, which many employers allow you to do.

This is partly because of the free employer contributions they will miss out on but also the lost compound interest.

"The current minimum pension age is 57, so any money you save in your 20s will have at least 30 years to compound and grow.

"£100 saved now, compounded at 4% a year over 30 years, is going to be worth a lot more than £100 saved in 15 to 20 years' time."

She also urges younger people to think ahead. "You really need to think of your future self and what that person will need to retire comfortably."

Kharlee, 47, a teacher from South East London, can certainly relate to this. She stopped her contributions to a workplace pension twice over the last five years for financial reasons.

And she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.

She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change.

"I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."

Are you able to save money every month? Share your tips with us on how you do it.

title: The wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fall
content:
At the lavish home of one of Miami's top plastic surgeons, overlooking the Biscayne Bay, some of the wealthiest Cuban-American families in Florida have gathered.

They are there to thrash out their vision of Cuba's future at the fourth meeting of the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC).

Rum in hand and Rolexes on wrists, this is Miami's old money. People with well-recognised Cuban-American surnames – like Bacardi and Babun – chat around the pool about the lamentable state of the island's economy, and share titbits of gossip about the latest political rumblings.

"The intention of this evening is to gather under one roof the most prominent Cuban-American entrepreneurs in Miami-Dade County," says CANCC president Juan Omar Sixto, "and the objective is to be in Cuba once the regime falls".

His guests are convinced that moment is nigh.

This influential community of Cuban exiles has detested the Communist-run government ever since the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro expropriated their lands and nationalised their families' companies after taking power in 1959.

And they have wielded their political and economic clout in Florida over the years to shape Washington's policies towards their homeland.

Sixto fled the island as a teenager. Now a real estate developer in his early 80s, his organisation is drafting plans for what he calls "the day after" in Cuba.

The CANCC has created a proposal for a Cuban Stock Exchange and formed committees on everything from energy infrastructure to food security.

Post-Communist planning is nothing new in Miami.

Countless documents and logistical plans have been drawn up by interest groups over the decades, some of them more sober and measured than others.

The difference now, insists Sixto, is the Trump administration's push to force total change on the island. And he says they have the ear of some high-profile contacts including people close to the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio.

"Together with deliveries of humanitarian aid and medical supplies, we'd go and do business in Cuba right away," says Sixto.

In Cuba itself, such claims are mostly met with scepticism.

In the face of Washington's "maximum pressure" campaign on Cuba, the island's leadership recently announced 176 economic liberalisation measures. The Cuban President, Miguel Díaz-Canel, said they were "to advance the defence of socialism, to support and widen social justice".

To his critics, they look distinctly like full-blown capitalism - lifting the cap on the number of workers in a private business, allowing the direct hiring and firing of Cuban employees and permitting ownership of multiple enterprises at once, including by Cuban Americans.

Still, the attendees at the CANCC meeting dismissed the economic reforms as cosmetic, saying they gave no meaningful guarantees to investors. They would "not put a foot into Cuba", Sixto said, while the current regime remained in place.

Some analysts think such planning meetings are premature. Although Cuban Americans are convinced that change is imminent in Cuba, none can say with any certainty what it will be - a US military operation as seen in Venezuela in January? Or a new economic pact with the island's leadership?

"Right now, the very high expectations created by the US administration that some kind of 'day after' was coming soon, or that Cuba would 'be next' have been kicked down the road," says Mike Bustamante, associate professor of history at the University of Miami.

With the November mid-term elections in the US approaching and the Trump administration embroiled in the "quagmire" of the Iran war, Bustamante argues there is little appetite for further foreign adventures.

"It's really tough to think that they will escalate further than what they're doing which is this drip-drip-drip of sanctions."

With the island's oil supply effectively shut off since January, that is already a significant escalation, says Mike Bustamente. Although they have made life unbearable for most ordinary people, they haven't yet "created the ingredients for a political inflection point" in Cuba, he adds.

The Cuban government has not commented on the CANCC itself. But traditionally such groups prompt indignation among revolutionaries who insist they will not be forced out by their critics in Miami.

I ask some guests if they can appreciate the irony that the same people who support a major source of the island's misery – the decades-long US economic embargo and the current fuel blockade – are now hatching plans for its reconstruction, without the input of most Cubans.

For Cuban-American agricultural expert Hugo Orizondo it is only practical to draw up a road map to Cuban development. "Right now, Cuba is like a black hole, we don't know what is happening over there," he admits. "But we do know the potential [for investment]."

Orizondo says he understands the reticence among Cubans to see foreign investors buying up something as sensitive as the rights to arable land. "But what are they going to do with it?" he retorts. "When investors come, they bring money and technology into the land."

Both are urgently needed, he says, if Cuba is ever to produce enough to feed its own population and break its reliance on food imports.

Land titles lie at the heart of any reconstruction project put forward by this generation of wealthy Cuban Americans. Juan Omar Sixto says his father lost five properties and a farm in Cuba's Pinar del Rio province to the revolution. While he insists he has no intention of removing any family living in those homes, he does want compensation for the nationalised land.

"I worked on that farm for five years of my life with my father, and they took it away. I want restitution or compensation. Even if they give me just a penny on the dollar, I'll take it."

"It's moral justice," he argues.

The Cuban government portrays such historic title claims as bitterness by a corrupt landed gentry who made fortunes on the backs of indentured workers and slaves. Both slavery and the system of indentured workers didn't end in Cuba until the late 19th Century.

The government also argues that the exiles could never stand that Castro passed land reforms which handed over their fields to the workers and the state.

"Most of our sugar mills have been dismantled, but we will recover those lands and put them into production," says Nicolás Gutiérrez, the president of the National Association of Sugar Mill Owners of Cuba, an exile organisation championing the title claims.

"I'm not promising it will be in sugar," he says.

"It might be in ethanol, co-generation, solar panels or water purification cells. Who knows? There are a lot of different options," he remarks. "We need to get them producing, we need to have a real wage paid to Cuban workers and create a multiplier economic effect across the island."

With the ice clinking in their drinks and a cool breeze rustling the palm trees on the perfectly manicured lawn, the CANCC members make it sound easy. But within hours of their gathering, Cuba had descended into its sixth nationwide blackout this year.

The disconnection between the hopes for change in Miami and the realities on the ground in Cuba is stark. Many Miami-based Cubans think the monumental shift they have prayed for is almost here.

If so, it will inevitably bring huge social and humanitarian disruption which the stricken island is ill-equipped to cope with. Even assuming the diaspora's support is well-intentioned rather than purely self-interested, fixing the island's failing electrical grid alone is estimated to cost $8bn to $10bn (£6bn to £7.5bn).

Before any industry in Cuba – from agriculture to tourism – can be revitalised by the exiles' wealth and political connections, Cubans continue to face acute shortages in food, water, fuel and medicines. Miami's ambitious plans aside, most Cubans just hope their days get a little easier sometime soon.

title: 传Anthropic最快11月中旬启动IPO 估值或达2万亿美元 拟在感恩节前登陆美股
content:
据知情人士透露，人工智能（AI）公司Anthropic正寻求最快于11月中旬启动首次公开募股（IPO），并争取在11月26日美国感恩节假期前正式登陆美股市场。尽管近期AI安全争议升温、竞争对手OpenAI推迟上市计划，Anthropic仍在推进IPO准备工作。部分潜在投资者认为，该公司的合理估值可能达到1.8万亿至2万亿美元。
知情人士表示，旗下拥有Claude系列AI模型的Anthropic最快可能于11月9日当周启动IPO正式推介程序，为感恩节前开始交易创造条件。由于美国资本市场的交易活动通常会在感恩节前后明显放缓，公司希望在假期前完成上市。
Anthropic此前已推迟原定上市安排，但知情人士称，公司目前仍预计最迟于今年年底完成上市。不过，相关讨论仍在进行中，具体时间表可能继续调整。
加速推进上市计划 10月14日拟与潜在投资者会面
Anthropic的上市准备工作正在逐步推进。据知情人士透露，公司计划于10月14日在旧金山总部与潜在投资者举行会议，为即将到来的IPO进行准备。此前有报道称，Anthropic原计划在夏季结束后公开提交IPO申请文件，但上市进程随后有所推迟。
按照目前讨论中的时间安排，公司可能在11月9日当周启动正式推介，并争取在11月26日感恩节之前完成股票上市交易。不过，知情人士强调，相关安排尚未最终确定，具体上市日期仍可能发生变化。
如果Anthropic能够按照目前的计划推进IPO，将意味着该公司在近期新股市场多家企业推迟上市的背景下，仍选择加快进入公开资本市场。
估值最高或达2万亿美元 IPO规模有望比肩SpaceX
尽管AI行业近期面临安全争议及竞争加剧等挑战，Anthropic的潜在投资者似乎仍对其长期发展前景抱有较高预期。部分知情人士透露，一些潜在投资者认为，Anthropic的合理估值可能在1.8万亿至2万亿美元之间。
此前有报道称，Anthropic预计此次IPO的募资规模有望达到或超过SpaceX（SPCX.US）创纪录的上市规模。如果相关估值预期最终得到市场认可，Anthropic将跻身全球市值最高的上市科技企业之列。
不过，目前披露的估值区间主要来自部分潜在投资者的判断，并不代表Anthropic已经确定IPO发行价格或最终估值。实际上市估值仍将取决于市场环境、投资者需求及发行安排。
2025年营收大幅增长 净亏损却接近420亿美元
Anthropic快速扩张的业务规模，是支撑其高估值预期的重要因素之一。不过，公司持续扩大的亏损也可能成为IPO过程中投资者重点关注的问题。根据此前披露的财务文件，Anthropic在2025年实现约46亿美元营收，较2024年的3.86亿美元大幅增长。与此同时，公司2025年净亏损接近420亿美元，约为2024年83亿美元净亏损的五倍。
不过，值得注意的是，Anthropic巨额净亏损并非全部来自日常经营支出。相关文件显示，2025年公司负债公允价值变动造成的损失超过340亿美元，占全年净亏损的绝大部分。
从经营层面来看，Anthropic同期营业亏损超过80亿美元，反映出公司在模型研发、算力基础设施及业务扩张方面仍承担着较高成本。
这意味着，虽然Anthropic的营收增长迅速，其商业模式距离实现稳定盈利仍存在挑战。对于潜在IPO投资者而言，如何评估高速增长的收入与持续高企的投入之间的关系，将是判断公司估值的重要因素。
OpenAI竞争压力回升 AI安全争议增添上市不确定性
除了财务表现，Anthropic还面临来自竞争对手的压力。今年以来，Anthropic在前沿AI模型市场的影响力持续提升，但近期OpenAI的销售增长势头有所增强，令双方竞争进一步加剧。
与此同时，一系列受到广泛关注的AI智能体网络攻击事件，引发公众对先进AI系统安全性的担忧，也增加了市场对相关企业上市前景的不确定性。
Anthropic首席执行官阿莫代伊近期在个人网站发表文章，主张放慢前沿AI模型的发展速度，以便更充分地应对潜在安全风险。其主要竞争对手OpenAI则已推迟IPO计划。OpenAI首席执行官Sam Altman表示，考虑到当前AI安全问题，此时推进上市并不明智。
与OpenAI选择暂缓上市不同，Anthropic目前仍在推动IPO进程，显示两家公司在资本市场安排上的不同选择。不过，AI安全问题是否会影响Anthropic的投资者需求、估值水平及最终上市时间，仍有待观察。
美股IPO市场表现分化 多家企业推迟上市
Anthropic筹备上市之际，美国IPO市场正面临一定压力。近期，多家企业因估值分歧或市场环境变化而推迟上市计划。其中，智能戒指制造商Oura成为数周内第三家在原定首次发行股票前数小时正式推迟上市的公司。此前，部分潜在投资者对其约150亿美元的完全稀释后估值目标表示疑虑。
与此同时，今年上市的新股整体表现也相对疲软。根据数据，如果剔除SpaceX和SK海力士创纪录的上市交易，今年超过100只新上市股票的加权平均回报率为负4%。相比之下，标普500指数今年以来上涨约12%，以科技股为主的纳斯达克100指数上涨约20%。
这一表现差距反映出，尽管美国大型科技股整体表现较强，新上市企业未必能够获得同等程度的市场追捧，投资者对IPO估值和盈利前景仍较为谨慎。
在这一背景下，Anthropic能否凭借快速增长的AI业务吸引足够的投资者需求，并获得市场对其高估值的认可，将成为其IPO推进过程中的重要看点。

title: Bellamy says Wales 'stick' hurt as Norway win lifts mood
content:
Head coach Craig Bellamy says he has been through a "really difficult" spell because of criticism aimed in his direction during Wales' winless run.

Bellamy's Wales claimed the finest result of his reign as they came from behind to beat Norway 2-1 at the Cardiff City Stadium on Thursday.

The victory ended a six-game winless run which began with defeat by Bosnia-Herzegovina in the World Cup play-off semi-final in March.

When asked whether Wales' success had lifted a weight off his shoulders, Bellamy revealed he had "felt the stick" ever since the Bosnia loss.

"The summer wasn't easy, then these games weren't easy," he said.

"But I've seen it; I've drawn on experience because I've seen managers before me get it.

"I've been part of that, and I've seen the abuse. I've seen the abuse the previous manager got just before me, and I have to be honest, it's been a really difficult couple of months."

Former Wales striker Bellamy, who was appointed national boss in July 2024, faced criticism from some fans after holding talks over a potential move to Burnley in June.

In a lengthy news conference after the Norway triumph, he said he feels people "could be kinder to each other" after revealing the negativity aimed at him had also affected his family.

"It's not me but I have kids and a wife; it's for them - they see it," he said.

"I've lived in this environment and I had it as a player, but I think there's ways we can speak to people and just because it's the game we love, it doesn't give us the right to think we can say whatever we want to.

"We're such a small country, why can't we have each other's backs? Why don't we look after each other more? Maybe that's me.

"I'm not saying everyone's above criticism, far from it. But I think it's too easy, and we're too quick."

Bellamy said he did not "want to spoil" the upbeat mood after Wales' morale-boosting win, which was the first against a nation ranked higher in the world since he took charge and the country's first in the top tier of the Nations League.

"I'm really happy with it, but I'm happy for the country, you understand?" he added.

"I give everything for my country. Everything. I turned down big money to keep doing this. I love doing this."

title: The Papers: 'Laughing criminals let loose' and 'Return to the castle'
content:
Spoiler warning: This press review reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

The Daily Telegraph warns the UK is "at risk of fuel shortages", external after President Donald Trump threatened to cut off US diesel shipments unless Europe released emergency reserves. The paper notes it is "unclear whether the UK would be directly included" in any threatened export ban, but that such a move would "rapidly increase pump prices". A Trump administration official tells the Financial Times it is "in Europe's best interests to work with the United States", external to boost supply and bring down costs. A Whitehall source quoted in the Times accuses Washington of "brazen negotiating tactics", external, and says reserve stocks are "there to act as a buffer against supply shortages".

The Guardian has been told that "ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes"., external They apparently include "scrapping the health element of universal credit for under 25s" and replacing it with a "multibillion-pound package of support to get into work". The government says it will not pre-empt the findings of two reviews due in the autumn and that it will "always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable".

Sources close to Number 10 have told the i Paper that holding a snap general election in May "has not been ruled out", external - despite Burnham's "insistence that there would not be one".

The Daily Mail declares Thursday's early release of prisoners in England and Wales the "first of ten tidal waves of convicts"., external The paper quotes a man freed from HMP Brixton as saying he is "gonna go stealing again". Another from Wandsworth Prison, on his way to "get some kebabs", says the early releases are "good" because the jail is "full".

The Sun calls Downing Street's clarification of the prime minister's position on Manchester City's dispute with the Premier League an "own goal"., external The paper says he was accused of "political interference" after saying he did not want to "lose" the club's owners. Number 10 has since said there cannot be "any suggestion that anyone is above the rules". City deny any wrongdoing.

title: 美联储理事库克称供应冲击影响意外持久 传统应对方式面临考验
content:
美联储理事丽莎·库克表示，供应冲击变得更加突出，其影响“意外持久”，这在考验美联储选择忽略这类冲击的传统做法。
库克周四在纽约联储主办的活动上表示：“供应冲击的影响意外持久，而且过去几年我们看到的供应冲击越来越多，因此它们变得更加突出”。
她表示：“我们过去的传统看法是会忽略这些供应冲击，因为收紧货币政策不会影响油价，也不会影响战争”。
库克在与纽约联储行长约翰·威廉姆斯共同出席的小组讨论中表示：“现在可能的情况是，取决于许多不同因素，对于何为最优的政策应对可能会得出不同结论”。
她表示，美联储需要确保通胀预期不会脱离锚定。
库克重申，她认为人工智能建设在增加通胀压力，而且这项技术何时才能带来生产力提升尚不明朗。
她表示：“我担心何时才会出现能够推动通胀降温的生产力提升，以及下一个供应瓶颈会在哪里”。

title: Andy Burnham searches for UK alternative to Palantir
content:
Chris Smyth , Lucy Fisher and Laura Hughes in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Andy Burnham’s government is searching for a UK alternative to Palantir, as the prime minister’s “Buy British” push triggers a hunt to find a homegrown replacement for the controversial US software group in the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.

Ministers have identified a handful of UK technology companies they hope might be candidates to take over the health service’s Federated Data Platform, as they consider applying a break clause in Palantir’s contract in March next year, people familiar with the matter told the FT.

Meanwhile, a defence minister has told parliament that the government is sounding out alternative suppliers for its MoD contract.

Some government figures are pushing to replace Palantir , which has come under fire over its links to the Trump administration and the US defence sector, to reduce the risk of a backlash by progressives against Burnham’s drive to foster the British AI industry.

Palantir won a £330mn contract from NHS England (NHSE) in 2023 to run the health service’s Federated Data Platform, a system designed to drive efficiencies and improve care in hospitals by joining up data better.

But the project has been beset by controversy, with NHSE claims about the success of the platform under growing scrutiny after the FT identified a litany of errors in a key underlying dataset.

This year, a minister was forced to apologise after the FT revealed some Palantir staff would have “unlimited access” to identifiable patient information while working on one part of the FDP, which NHSE had failed to disclose.

One option under consideration is to offer Palantir a temporary contract extension of about 12 months to give more time to develop a British alternative, according to people familiar with discussions. The current contract stipulates a minimum two-year extension from March.

Ministers are also considering whether the FDP programme could be divided between several companies, rather than run solely by Palantir.

Quantexa, which was in the running for the FDP contract in 2023, is among three or four British tech companies being considered, according to people familiar with discussions. The others are not known.

However, no decisions have yet been taken, and some Labour figures argue that Palantir’s UK-based business should be considered a British company under Burnham’s definition.

Tom Bartlett, former deputy director of data engineering and integration at NHS England, said it would be “hugely risky” to replace Palantir and “a leap into the unknown”.

“There isn’t a platform that can replace the functionality that Palantir can bring,” he said. “They [the NHS and government] can assemble a group of people who are confident they could do it, but they would be proving themselves for the first time and it would be a gamble.”

While the government began a review of Palantir’s contract when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, a specific search for a British alternative is under way after Burnham said he wanted more government spending to go to UK businesses.

“I don’t think we should allow the culture of sending everything outside of this country to continue — this will be a big change under this government,” he said in his first House of Commons appearance as prime minister.

At the Labour Party conference in Liverpool this week, first secretary of state Louise Haigh said the government wanted to build “sovereign capabilities” in AI and boost the UK tech sector. This would ensure the country would not “be in hock to foreign giants”, she added.

One Labour figure confirmed that Haigh’s intervention was “a shot across the bows” at Palantir, adding: “There’s a wider question here about building up sovereign capabilities and capacity — and we do have world-leading UK expertise in this area.” The person said there was a general sense among officials that the UK state was “overly reliant on Palantir and overseas capabilities more widely”.

The Cabinet Office, which runs the machinery of government, has recently reviewed its public procurement rules and rewritten the “social value” requirements to focus more narrowly on UK job creation and skills development.

However, officials have stressed that these criteria are legally “country agnostic”: while they favour companies supporting British jobs and training, that does not have to mean British-owned groups.

Another government figure said there was a particular focus on sovereign capabilities in health technologies, which ministers hoped could transform the NHS while fostering an industry based on its rich data sets.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan told a Politico event on the sidelines of Labour’s conference that polling consistently showed “the British public wants to make sure that their private data, particularly in healthcare, isn’t in the hands of foreign billionaires and foreign firms abroad”.

James Frith, the health innovation minister, told MPs last month that he was “concerned about mistrust of Palantir and the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.

Questions about Palantir’s involvement in the health service are seen as more acute than its work with the MoD, according to officials, but it is also being examined.

In November 2022, Palantir was awarded a three-year contract by the MoD worth £75.2mn after the tender was not advertised. In December 2025, the company was directly awarded another three-year contract, again without any competition, worth £240.6mn.

Speaking in June, in response to questions on the contract, defence minister Lord Vernon Coaker said: “We are seeking to look at options with small and medium-sized and other companies that could provide the same capability, so that we have a competitive process in future.”

The process would “keep Palantir on its toes in the marketplace as well”, he added.

Other European governments are seeking to cut their reliance on American technology providers amid growing concern over US President Donald Trump’s foreign policy.

France and Germany have excluded or cut contracts with Palantir from their armed forces and intelligence agencies in recent months, seeking more local alternatives.

Palantir said in a statement that its software was “helping to deliver better care” and that it was “deeply committed to the UK”.

“More than one in six of our global workforce is based here . . . And all UK government data is stored in the UK,” it added. The Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

An MoD spokesperson said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, we will bring forward a package of ‘backing British’ measures to ensure that defence spending is driving value back into local communities, while remaining consistent with our international obligations.

“We continue to work with a range of international suppliers based on operational requirements, including Palantir, which is a longstanding technology investor in the UK economy.”

title: Chris Mason: Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
content:
The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.

The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it.

It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world – because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.

Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan.

The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level.

Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.

All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.

His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.

He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.

One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.

It is worth quoting his answer in full.

"Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."

His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".

Firstly, his fear – being "really concerned" – that the vast money from Abu Dhabi, that has transformed not just the club but parts of the city, could go.

Secondly, that "I can't intervene more" in the process that is ongoing. What does "more" mean?

To be fair, as you can see in the full quote above and he said repeatedly elsewhere in the interview, he was trying to be circumspect about it all.

"I am not getting directly involved in the process," he told me, later adding "I have to keep my distance from it."

But, the cumulative impression many were left with was that he was sympathetic to Manchester City's situation, not least because he repeatedly compared it to a vastly smaller row involving his own club Everton's finances a few years ago.

"I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time, and you know, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn't fair the way that was handled. So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."

Everton were docked Premier League points over it.

Despite the gravity and breadth of what Manchester City now confront, Andy Burnham offered no explicit criticism of them.

The back pages and the sports channels as well as news sites and social media were quickly ablaze with the remarks.

And by teatime on Thursday, No10 were back-pedalling.

A written statement was sent out, which again is worth quoting in full:

"As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Some 59 words that could be replaced by a picture of a reversing light – the tone and language completely different from Burnham's to me on camera.

But even that statement didn't last long. Immediately, the first word of the second paragraph of it was jumped on. "If."

Remember, the Premier League says Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of almost a billion pounds. The club deny wrongdoing and are considering an appeal, but the Premier League's conclusion is clear.

But Downing Street said "if." Fast forward a little over an hour, and the statement was re-issued. "If" became "wherever."

In real time, No10's jitters and discomfort about this was there for all to see.

The prime minister seen as Mr Manchester, who loves his football and revels in a man of the people image, caught up in one of the biggest domestic stories of the year and one that is only just beginning.

It won't be the last time he faces questions about Manchester City.
